results.headline: After the 2021 federal pay change, new rural health clinics (RHCs) switched from hospital-owned to for-profit freestanding. The for-profit share of new enrollments went from 27% in 2020 to 56% in 2023. For-profit freestanding clinics went from 6.4 a month to 13.5 a month. One chain, Fast Pace, holds 189 clinics under 48 NPIs, all enrolled from 2021-11-23 on: 26% of the new for-profit freestanding clinics. NPI 1316602774 is FAST PACE MEDICAL CLINIC PLLC, TN, 75 clinics.
results.checked: I read the date built into ENROLLMENT_ID and counted new enrollments by month, split by CCN class and for-profit flag. CCN digits 3400-3499, 3975-3999 and 8500-8899 mean provider-based; 3800-3974 and 8900-8999 mean freestanding. I checked the class against the hospital enrollment file by ASSOCIATE_ID: 97.2% of nonprofit provider-based clinics have a hospital owner, against 0.8% of for-profit freestanding ones, and the state agrees on 99% of hits. Then I grouped the post-July-2021 for-profit freestanding clinics by owner.
results.hit_means: An urgent-care chain turned its storefronts into Medicare rural health clinics right after Congress raised the independent-clinic pay cap (Consolidated Appropriations Act 2021, from April 2021; confirm the rule text). One chain took a quarter of the new for-profit slots.
results.miss_means: If Fast Pace's clinics predated 2021 or were hospital-owned, it would be the ordinary case of hospital systems running many clinics.
results.boring: Hospital systems owning many RHCs: true for provider-based clinics, ruled out for Fast Pace (freestanding, for-profit). Survivorship, since the file holds only currently enrolled clinics: that shrinks old years evenly and does not explain the switch in type, so partly ruled out. The law working as intended (more rural clinics): not ruled out; that is the frame, and the story is who captures the higher rate. No year-end-2020 grandfathering rush: December 2020 had 34 provider-based enrollments against about 25 a month.
traps: CCN digits code provider-based vs freestanding. Confirmed by the hospital-enrollment join (97% vs 0.8%).
No RHC owner file is in the warehouse, so private-equity ownership cannot be tested.
The enrollment ID date is when the enrollment was created. A change of owner may re-date it.

results.headline: Houston, not LA. Five certified hospices sit in one suite, 7322 Southwest Fwy Suite 610, 'Room A' to 'Room E', certified 2023-04-13 to 2023-06-08. Four share (281) 410-1013. Eight hospices with eight brand names and four owner IDs share (713) 874-1234; six of them are in one Rosedale St building. 16.7% of Harris County hospices share a phone with another hospice, against 4.5% nationally and 2.9% in LA. Clark County, NV is still growing: 25% certified since 2024, against 6% nationally.
results.checked: I stripped phone numbers to 10 digits and counted hospices that share a phone with another certified hospice, by county, next to certification-year buckets. Denominator: all certified hospices in the county. I listed every phone behind 3 or more hospices, joined those hospices by CCN to the hospice enrollment file for owner ID and incorporation date (5,976 of 6,852 CCNs land), and listed every hospice in the four Houston buildings.
results.hit_means: Several licenses with different names, owner IDs and even lettered 'rooms' share one phone line and one suite. That is the hospice-mill signature, and all of them are on the current certified roster.
results.miss_means: If the shared phones were only real chains under one brand (Moments, Agape, Beacon, Brighton, Harbor), it would be ordinary central scheduling.
results.boring: A shared answering or billing service owning the phone: not ruled out, though five licenses in one lettered suite is hard to explain that way. LA hospice fraud is widely covered; Houston's clusters and Las Vegas's growth since 2024 are less covered, but Texas prosecutions exist. Partly new.
traps: (909) 000-0000 is a filler phone on 4 San Bernardino hospices.
876 of 6,852 certified CCNs (13%) have no row in the hospice enrollment file, so they have no owner ID.
The warehouse has no hospice owner file.

results.headline: Reliant Care Management (MO/KS, 32 homes) drew 3.37x the harm-level citations per bed of its own states: 152 against 45.2 expected, 70 at immediate jeopardy (J-L), with harm on 2 or more separate surveys at 19 of 32 homes. Bria Health Services (IL, 15 homes): 195 against 81.7 (2.39x). Plainview 3.43x, Hurlbut 8.19x (small counts), Ephram Lahasky 2.49x. The median chain sits at 0.98x; 14 of about 300 chains reach 2x or more.
results.checked: I read the severity letters first: 23,087 harm-level G-L citations, 9,661 of them J-L. I lined up years on the penalty file's window (2023-06-17 to 2026-05-13) and kept 19,953 G-L citations. I computed each state's harm citations per certified bed. Each chain's expected count = its beds x its own states' rates, from CMS's CHAIN_ID joined by padded CCN. I compared observed to expected, with fines from the penalty file.
results.hit_means: A mid-size chain draws 2-3x the harm citations its own states hand out per bed, across most of its homes, on separate visits.
results.miss_means: With O/E near 1, the chain is as bad as its neighbors, and the count only reflects size or state strictness.
results.boring: State survey strictness: ruled out by the own-state per-bed comparison, which also covers the Illinois flag trap for Bria. One bad survey making many tags: ruled out for Reliant and Bria (repeat surveys), not for Hurlbut. Chain label is CMS's current one, so homes bought after their citations count toward the new chain; the CHOW flag is a constant, so timing cannot be checked: not ruled out. The triage angle 'never pay' is dead: harm-cited homes in these chains are fined more often than their states predict (Reliant 2 unfined against 6.8 expected), and the file records fines imposed, not paid.
traps: FED_CMS_NURSING_HOME.CHAIN_ID is never null, so independents carry some other value. The '300 chains' may include one independents bucket. Unresolved.
The penalty file starts 2023-06-17, while citations go back to 2017. Line up the windows.

results.headline: 94 ex-members of Congress (names unique among legislators, left office 1970 or later) filed FARA short forms after leaving office. 26 first filed in 2017 or later. 5 filed in 2025: Robert Wexler (Ballard Partners), Rod Blagojevich (RRB Strategies, Bosnia & Herzegovina), Chris Stewart (Skyline Capitol), Chaka Fattah (Blackwood International, Liberia) and John Seymour (weak match). Since 2017, Ukraine drew the most US registrants (89), then Qatar (85). This is a known story, and there are no dollars in the pull.
results.checked: I split the four stacked files (RegistrantDocs 152,224, ShortForms 44,508, ForeignPrincipals 17,663, Registrants 7,060). I read the active flag (807 active principals, all with no termination date). I counted distinct registrants per country by principal registration date. Then I joined short-form first+last names to Congress legislators, kept names held by one legislator only, and required the short form to come after the member's last term ended.
results.hit_means: Ex-members keep registering as foreign agents, including two 2025 filers with federal convictions on the public record.
results.miss_means: If the matches were mostly common-name collisions, there would be no list. Firms named for the member (Moran Global, Waxman Consulting, Nickles Group, Breaux Lott, RRB) confirm many of them.
results.boring: OpenSecrets Foreign Lobby Watch and POGO already track the revolving door, and the 2025 names made news. Not ruled out. There is at least one sure false match: 'Stephanie Jones' filed in 2019, but Stephanie Tubbs Jones died in office in 2008. A few common names are doubtful.
traps: REGISTRANT_NAME is empty in the Registrants and ForeignPrincipals files. The firm name sits in PERSON_NAME in the Registrants file.
There are no dollar columns in any of the four files.
Short-form dates include junk like 1900-01-07.

results.headline: The star angle is weak. 21.3% of 1-star hospitals (10 of 47) vs 8.3% of 5-star (6 of 72) paid one officer more than their charity care, and 1-star top officers earn less ($437K median vs $512K). The real catch is for F-003: 141 of its 249 hits (57%) are unrated hospitals with a median of 25 beds and 242 discharges. Among rated hospitals, F-003's 27% drops to 16% (108 of 676).
results.checked: I read the rating values and footnotes: 3,182 rated, 2,250 unrated (41.4%); footnote 16 is too few measures, mostly critical-access hospitals. I rebuilt F-003's 919-hospital nonprofit set from its own SQL (2022 990 officer pay against 2022 HCRIS charity care) and joined it on CCN = FACILITY_ID. Land rate 919 of 919; state agrees 919 of 919. Then I compared by star.
results.hit_means: Low stars going with officers out-earning charity care would tie quality to pay priorities.
results.miss_means: If pay tracked stars, 1-star executives would earn more. They earn less, and the 1-star vs 5-star gap rests on 10 vs 6 hospitals.
results.boring: Size drives it: 5-star hospitals are bigger (198 beds) with bigger charity budgets. Not ruled out. Tiny rural hospitals, where one $226K salary tops a $133K charity line, carry most of F-003's headline.
traps: F-003's 27% leans on tiny unrated hospitals: 57% of its hits. Among star-rated hospitals it is 16%.
There is no system or chain field, so 'clusters in chains' cannot be tested from this table.

results.headline: The UK sanctions 620 ships under its Russia rules, and 358 of them (58%) are not on the US OFAC SDN list. 309 of those 358 were designated in 2024-2025, at least 6 months before the SDN pull (2026-06-25). Across all regimes: 657 UK ships, 291 on the SDN, 366 UK-only. OpenSanctions gets the same answer independently: 658 UK vessels, 291 also on the SDN. 8 UK-only tankers pinged in US waters Jan 1-8 2024 under their old names (e.g. NOBLE was SCF NEVA; PIERRE was SEA VINE, with 8,422 pings off Southern California), all before the UK designated them. These are data matches, not verified.
results.checked: [12] Took the 7-digit IMO from every UK ship row and joined it to SDN IMOs (IMO column, or REMARKS when blank): 2,030 SDN IMOs. [24] Counted OpenSanctions targets tagged UK FCDO, and how many are also tagged US OFAC SDN, by type. [13] Grouped NOAA AIS by IMO, then joined it to the UK IMOs. [25] Second-field check on the 8 AIS hits: names, type, flag.
results.hit_means: The UK/US split on shadow-fleet ships is big (358 ships) and two independent joins confirm it. People and companies split the same way: 42% of UK-listed persons and 43% of companies are not on the SDN.
results.miss_means: It never got a miss. A gap under 10% would have meant a timing lag between lists.
results.boring: US policy slowed new Russia designations in 2025, and trade press (Lloyd's List and others) has covered this gap. Not ruled out; it is the likely reason. The AIS join only shows history from before designation, because the warehouse holds 8 days of AIS (Jan 1-8 2024). It goes live only with longer AIS or port-call data showing post-sanction US calls.
traps: Ship rows have only 15 distinct OFSI_GROUP_ID across 657 ships. Key ships on IMO or DESIGNATION_ID.
IMO_NUMBER comes in mixed formats ('9114555' and 'IMO9276561'). Pull the 7 digits with a regex.
Names do not survive renames: 108 of 291 IMO matches to the SDN disagree on name, and so do 8 of 8 AIS hits. The UK list has no alias rows for those hulls, so IMO is the only link.
Row count is not target count: alias rows repeat each designation (DPRK ship 9114555 has 30 rows).

results.headline: This is the XC UK list again, with broken dates. 5,127 OFSI group IDs appear in both tables, 2 only here and 1 only in XC. LAST_UPDATED has day and month swapped in 4,352 of 4,391 comparable IDs, and 95 IDs are dated in the future (RUS3601 reads 2026-11-05 here, 2026-05-11 in XC). DATE_DESIGNATED is filled for only 1,776 of 6,334 IDs.
results.checked: [1-2] Counted rows and looked at a sample. [5] Full outer join of distinct OFSI_GROUP_ID against XC. [15] Joined UNIQUE_ID to XC DESIGNATION_ID (6,315 of 6,334 match) and compared LAST_UPDATED and DATE_DESIGNATED, including a day/month swap test.
results.hit_means: It is a duplicate of XC with worse dates, so there is no separate story. Every angle belongs to XC.
results.miss_means: If the two tables had diverged, one would hold targets the other lacks. They don't.
results.boring: Same OFSI file, loaded twice by two pipelines, with one parsing dd/mm as mm/dd. Ruled in.
traps: LAST_UPDATED is day/month-swapped: 4,352 of 4,391 comparable IDs swapped, 95 in the future. About 1,924 matched IDs have no comparable date (my read: the day was over 12, so the swap didn't parse). Use the XC table.
DATE_DESIGNATED is mostly blank here (1,776 of 6,334 IDs) but filled on every XC row.

results.headline: In a fixed set of 1,906 counties with jail data in 2010, 2015, 2019 and 2023, rural jails went 531 to 624 per 100K residents aged 15-64 (2010 to 2019), then back to 563 in 2023. Urban jails fell 335 to 227, so by 2023 the rural rate is 2.5x the urban. The top growers are mostly contract jails: Karnes TX went 106 to 454 people with 89% held for fed/prison, Fannin TX 83%, Baker FL 81% including 272 ICE. The local-growth leads are Butts GA (136 to 354 to 554, 0% held, 3x its suburban-Georgia peers, 1.12x over rated capacity in 2019) and Yazoo MS (95 to 378, 1% held). Data matches, not verified.
results.checked: [8] Jail fill by year. [21] Pooled jail rate by urbanicity for the fixed cohort; rate = jail pop / residents aged 15-64 x 100K. [28] Growers 2010 to 2019 among 1,276 counties with 10K+ residents aged 15-64 and 100+ in jail in 2019. Each county is compared to the median of its state + urbanicity peers (national median growth 1.07x), alongside its held-for-others share and capacity. [22] was a first try; it is void because the held columns go blank after 2020.
results.hit_means: There are named counties whose jails grew 2.5-4x while their peers stayed flat. Butts GA and Yazoo MS grew without holding anyone for other agencies.
results.miss_means: Without a fixed cohort, the post-2019 collapse in county coverage fakes a national decline. The fixed cohort shows the rural rise is real in Vera's numbers.
results.boring: Vera published the rural jail boom itself. The top growers hold federal or state prisoners (ruled in for the top 4). Butts GA and Yazoo MS are not explained by holds. The 'while crime fell' part was not tested: there is no county crime table in the plain catalog.
traps: County coverage collapses after 2019: about 2,900 counties in 2019, about 2,200 in 2020-23, 1,441 in 2024, 860 in 2025, 597 in 2026. 2025-26 are marked stub years. Always use a fixed cohort.
TOTAL_JAIL_FROM_ICE is empty from 2024, and all prison columns are empty from 2020.
Held-for-others columns can exceed total jail pop (Decatur GA 2010: 415 held vs 130 in jail) and go blank after 2020. Never subtract them across that break.
Before 1999, only 1970, 1978, 1983, 1988 and 1993 have near-full county jail coverage; other years have about 800-1,100 counties.
Race jail columns (BLACK_JAIL_POP etc.) are text, and COUNT() counts blanks. Use try_to_double.
Hardee FL 2010 jail = 10 people for 17.7K residents looks broken, which makes a fake 15x growth.

results.headline: This table is a copy of the Vera table: 0 differences on total jail pop, Black jail pop, Black rate and Black working-age pop across 128,507 county-years. Take 356 counties with 5K+ Black working-age residents and 20+ Black and 20+ white people in jail every year. Their median Black/white jail-rate ratio went 4.57 (2010) to 3.41 (2019) to 3.86 (2023), and counties at 10x+ went 30 to 19 to 24. So the gap narrowed until 2019 and widened after, but the widening crosses a data-source break. The 2019 top (599 counties, national median 3.2x) is Richmond NY 45.6x (NY median 7.4), New York County 29.3x, Arlington VA 22.1x (VA median 3.1). Data matches, not verified.
results.checked: [23] Joined county-year to Vera and counted disagreements. [19] 2019 ratio ranking with state-peer medians, plus the fed/prison share from Vera. [20] Fixed-cohort median and pooled ratio, 2010-2023. [29] Biggest ratio risers 2019 to 2023, plus the 5 NYC boroughs in 2019. Rates are per 100K residents aged 15-64.
results.hit_means: A named county jails Black residents at a ratio far above its state peers.
results.miss_means: With tiny denominators filtered out, most counties sit at 2-5x. The 2.1M-per-100K extremes are small-population noise.
results.boring: Vera publishes these ratios. NYC is one city jail system split by Vera across 5 boroughs (sum 12,718 in 2019, which looks high against the city's own headcount; not pulled, unverified). After 2020, white counts halve while totals hold (Miami-Dade white 421 to 201, total 4,184 to 4,278; Montgomery MD white 295 to 146, total 753 to 893; East Baton Rouge white 352 to 82). That looks like race-coding change, not behavior. Not ruled out.
traps: RACIAL_JAIL_DISPARITY is Vera re-served: 0 differences over 128,507 county-years. Don't count it as independent confirmation.
Rates use residents aged 15-64 as the denominator, not total population.
Coverage of Black rates falls from about 2,700 counties (2019) to about 1,100 (2020-23) and 56 (2024).
NYC borough values are Vera's allocation of one city jail system, and they top the disparity list.
Post-2020 white jail counts halve in several big counties while totals hold. It is likely race coding, so don't read it as a widening gap.

results.headline: There are 1,146 US healthcare posts on gang leak sites, 1,050 of them since 2024. 33 posts (2.9%) land on a Medicare hospital (CMS Hospital General) by exact cleaned name: 32 hospitals. That is about 4 in 10 of the roughly 79 posts whose title looks like a hospital name. 31 of the 33 names are unique in CMS. Watsonville Community Hospital was posted by two gangs 10 months apart (termite 2024-12, sinobi 2025-10), and The Loretto Hospital by two gangs 3 weeks apart. 224 US victims were posted by 2+ gangs, 16 of them healthcare. Data matches, not verified.
results.checked: [10-11] Counted rows and looked at a sample. [16][27] Counts by year: blank country, bulk timestamps, hospital-like titles. [17] US posts by sector. [18] Exact cleaned-name join of US healthcare post titles to HEALTH__FED_CMS_HOSPITAL_GENERAL (5.4K hospitals), showing city and state for eyeballing. [26] Same cleaned title posted by 2+ different gangs.
results.hit_means: Leak-site posts can be tied to named Medicare hospitals, many in small towns, which sets up a disclosure check.
results.miss_means: The other 97% of healthcare posts are clinics, labs, billing firms, or domain-only titles that exact-name matching can't place.
results.boring: A leak-site claim is not a confirmed breach. Healthcare ransomware is heavily covered, and 'small hospitals get hit' is known. Not ruled out. The 'did they report to HHS' angle is blocked: the HHS OCR breach portal is not in the warehouse. Hospital type (rural or critical access) was not pulled.
traps: COUNTRY is blank for 87% of 2021 rows, 80% of 2022 and 56% of 2023, against about 6% from 2024 on. Any US trend across 2023 to 2024 is a fill artifact.
Bulk timestamps: 168 rows in 2023 and 66 in 2024 share one DISCOVERED stamp with 50+ others.
The repeat-victim keys include redacted titles ('*************', 'C???o???m').
Unresolved: the fact line says maersk.com, fedex.com and renault.fr have 182 rows each, but an exact WEBSITE match finds 4 rows total. Probably variant spellings; not chased.
POST_TITLE is often a bare domain, so name joins undercount.

results.headline: White Birch Apartments in Milwaukee (339 units, 223% of fair market rent): HUD spends $2,574 per unit per month against a national median of $859 (3.0x). A second HUD file confirms the ratio, and the owner join lands 766 of 766 contracts.
results.checked: 24,309 contracts. Active contracts with a real ratio: 23,341, holding 1,458,275 units, median ratio 94. Over 150% of FMR: 766 contracts, 60,873 units (3.3%). Of those, 355 are elderly or disabled (202/811) buildings in cheap markets, 207 are family buildings in cheap markets, and 119 are in Puerto Rico. The HUD owners landing file joined on PROPERTY_ID: 766 of 766 land, and names agree on all 766. HUD's Picture of Subsidized Households (Dec 2025): the first word of CODE is the PROPERTY_ID, and unit counts agree within 10% on 97% of matches. Real spending per unit per month: in pricey markets, over-150% properties run $1,922 against $1,200 for peers, and 137 of 250 are over twice the national median. In cheap markets outside Puerto Rico: $933 against $670, with 18 of 326 over twice the median. Over-150% properties hold about 4.3% of units and take about 7.5% of matched spending, $1.30B a year. White Birch: new 240-month contract from 2023-12-01. Owner Aspen Crossing LIHTC LLC, manager Evergreen Real Estate Services (data match, not verified). Also checked: Lands End II NYC $5,294 (6.2x), Bicentennial Towers Detroit $1,726, Marshall Field Garden Chicago $2,559.
results.hit_means: HUD pays two to six times the national per-unit median on named buildings. Two separate HUD files agree on it, and the owner is on record.
results.miss_means: If the ratio were a bedroom-mix or FMR-date artifact, the spending file would show normal dollars. For the buildings named, it doesn't.
results.boring: Rents over FMR can be legal. After an owner recapitalizes, HUD can reset rents to cover the owner's budget or to match comparable buildings, and neither method is tied to FMR. Elderly buildings with services cost more. Puerto Rico FMRs are very low, and Manhattan rents beat the metro FMR. White Birch's new 20-year contract with a tax-credit (LIHTC) owner fits a recapitalization. NOT ruled out: this is the hinge. In cheap markets the lead is about 20 buildings, not 766.
traps: The 'dollars over FMR' in the SQL are my estimates ((ratio/100-1) x units x FMR x 12): $737M a year for over-150%, $2.68B for everything over 100%. Use the Picture of Subsidized Households spending field for real dollars.
RENT_TO_FMR_RATIO = 0 means unknown (298 rows), plus 81 nulls. FMR_xBR = 0 means the contract has no units of that size, not a $0 rent.
Join key confirmed: the first word of the Picture of Subsidized Households CODE equals the Section 8 PROPERTY_ID.

results.headline: TRI 2023 plants per 100 km2: D areas 13.35, B areas 2.21, A areas 0.07. D is denser than B in 119 of 212 cities. The join works, but the story is already published and the plants probably predate the maps.
results.checked: 10,154 shapes in 314 city-state pairs. GeoJSON is present on every row and 1 fails to parse. Point-in-shape join to 21,856 TRI 2023 plants (one point per TRIFD, longitude forced negative, pounds only): 1,549 land (7.1%). Per 100 km2: A 0.07 (1 plant), B 2.21, C 5.82, D 13.35, ungraded 25.46 (717 plants). Pounds released: D 23.0M, C 7.8M, B 1.5M, ungraded 29.1M. Same-city test across 212 cities with both B and D areas: D denser in 119, B in 17, both zero in 76. Top D-area releasers: Cleveland-Cliffs Cleveland Works 7.63M lbs, Phillips 66 Bayway 2.84M, BP Whiting 1.95M, EQ Detroit 1.54M.
results.hit_means: A 1930s D grade still predicts about 6x the plants and 13.6x the pounds per km2 of a B grade in 2023, and it holds within cities.
results.miss_means: No gradient would kill the angle. There is a gradient.
results.boring: The biggest D-area plants are century-old refinery and steel sites, so graders likely marked those neighborhoods D because industry was already there. Ungraded shapes (HOLC left industrial land ungraded) are the densest of all. The 1930s area notes that would settle this didn't load. Redlining-to-pollution research is already published. NOT ruled out.
traps: FIPS is one blank value on every row. HOLC_ID and YEAR_MAPPED are empty. AREA_DESCRIPTION_DATA is '{}' on every row, so the written grading reasons never loaded.
HOLC_GRADE text has stray spaces and E/F grades. Use HOLC_GRADE_RANK.
A grade join that drops null-grade shapes loses 717 of the 1,549 matched TRI plants. The ungraded shapes are the industrial areas.

results.headline: The angle is backwards. D.R. Horton's lender charged a median 3.99% vs 6.00% at other lenders: 1.72 points lower in the same county, with 59.3% of its loans at exactly 3.99%. In growth counties like Manatee FL (49.5%) and Denton TX (47.3%), builder lenders made about half of FHA purchase loans.
results.checked: 61,647 loans, one per ID. All are Purchase loans, all endorsed June 2026, no blank rates. 16 builder-lender brands tagged by name: 12.1% of loans. DHI: 3,791 loans. Median 3.99 vs 6.00. 88.3% under 5% vs 5.7% for everyone else. Same-county gap across 348 counties: -1.72 points and +$26,156 loan. Lennar: 1,973 loans, -1.58 points, -$9,919. Every builder brand is lower in the same county (-0.30 to -1.72 points). Of 129 counties with 100+ loans, 20 have a builder share above 29%, against 12.1% nationally.
results.hit_means: In Sun Belt growth counties, close to half of FHA purchase loans come from the builder's own lender at a bought-down rate.
results.miss_means: The triage premise that builder borrowers pay higher rates is dead: they pay about 1.7 points less.
results.boring: Builder rate buydowns and D.R. Horton's 3.99% FHA offers are already reported. New homes cost more than resales, which explains the bigger loans; there is no new-vs-existing flag, so that's not ruled out. One month of data.
traps: One month only (June 2026) and Purchase loans only. ENDORSEMENT_YEAR and ENDORSEMENT_MONTH are constants.
Builder lenders barely use down-payment help: DHI 0.1%, Lennar 0.0%, against 1.8% for everyone else. NVR (2.9%) is the exception.

results.headline: 56,159 rural units (13.5%) sit in projects opened by 1980 with no live affordability clause, and 35,324 of them get rent help. Iowa is at 36%, Missouri 32%, Wisconsin and Illinois 31%. The loan's due date isn't in the table, so this is a proxy for a problem that's already known.
results.checked: 13,550 projects, 417,524 units. 6.6% vacant. 282,739 units with rental help. Restrictive-use date: already past on 6,400 projects (184,580 units, 44%), none on 802, now through 2030 on 1,004 projects (31,911 units, 23,900 with rental help), 2031-35 on 1,260 projects (40,978 units). The dates follow a formula (about 20 or 50 years after opening). Proxy for loan maturity: 50 years from opening. By state, against 13.5% nationally: IA 36.1%, MO 31.9%, WI 30.7%, IL 30.6%, ME 27.9%. Vacancy: MS 10.1%, IL 9.4%, IA 9.3%, against 6.6%.
results.hit_means: Tens of thousands of rural rent-help units can leave the program when their loans are paid off, concentrated in the Midwest.
results.miss_means: With no real loan due date, the count stays a proxy, not a finding.
results.boring: USDA and housing groups already track and publish the maturing Section 515 mortgage problem. A past restrictive date doesn't mean exit, because the outstanding loan still binds the project. Not ruled out.
traps: 33 'active' projects list 100% vacancy. They are mostly seasonal migrant farm-labor centers (Lodi 94 units, Patterson 92, Arvin 88, Shafter 88) and 1-unit on-farm housing, caught off-season. Not abandonment.
DATE_RESTRICTIVE_CLAUSE_EXPIRES is formulaic and already past on 44% of units in 'active' projects. There is no loan maturity column.
22 tax-credit dates are placeholders (before 1987 or after 2080). The newest opening date is 2019-09-11. The source date isn't in the table.

results.headline: The top 10 lenders hold 59.7% of FY2020-26 FHA apartment insurance ($90.3B, 4,661 deals), with Greystone and Dwight Capital at 10% each. NYCHA PACT deals total $1.36B over 5 FHA numbers. The SAM join lands 1 of 21,225 projects.
results.checked: 25,557 rows but 24,819 FHA numbers. Raw sum $307.85B vs $298.32B at one row per FHA number: $9.5B double-counted. FY2020-26 Finally Endorsed, deduped: 88 lenders, top 10 at 59.7%. PACT: 3 NYCHA bundles via NYC HDC, HFA risk-sharing loans funded through the federal bank (FFB), Dec 2021: Linden-Penn Wortman $377.3M, Williamsburg $298.7M + $150M, Boulevard-Belmont $331.1M + $200M, on 5,205 units. SAM exclusions on normalized exact names: 0 lender hits. 1 project-plus-state hit: Lake Village of Auburn Hills MI, a $36.7M refinance in 2008 (Greystone). SAM shows a HUD voluntary exclusion from 2015-05-06, still active, 7 years after the loan (data match, not verified).
results.hit_means: A few lenders run most FHA apartment insurance, and NYCHA's conversions to private management (PACT) draw $1.36B of it.
results.miss_means: The barred-owner angle has nothing to stand on: the table has no owner names, and the join finds 1 project hit.
results.boring: The concentration among a few lenders is known. The PACT deals top the list because they are 1,600-1,900-unit campuses, and PACT financing is already reported.
traps: MORTGAGE_AMOUNT sums double-count reissued commitments: 738 extra rows, $9.5B. Dedupe on FHA_NUMBER first.
The fact line's 'PACT Williamsburg Houses 1.3B' counts FHA 01298082 three times and 01298113 twice. The real figure is $448.7M.

results.headline: 117 big community water systems (10K+ people) serving 8.73M have no sanitary survey on file in 5 years. The federal clock is 3 years, and on that clock 713 of 4,622 big systems (15.4%, 43.2M people) are past due. The gaps bunch up in CA (29.4%) and NJ (26.1%), while TN sits at 3.4%. Passaic Valley's last survey was 2014, and Jersey City MUA and Trenton Water Works were last surveyed in 2015.
results.checked: For every active community system, took the latest full, partial or follow-up sanitary survey date (SNSV, SNSP, SNSF), with the 1900 placeholder dates dropped. Joined that to the system roster on PWSID for people served. Counted systems with nothing since 2021-07-01 (5 years) and since 2023-07-01 (3 years), by state, then listed the largest.
results.hit_means: Big utilities have gone 5 to 12 years with no sanitary survey logged with EPA, bunched in CA and NJ while peer states run near zero. Every state reports surveys (96.9% of community systems have one since 2021-07), so the gap sits at named systems, not a missing state upload.
results.miss_means: Big systems all current, with overdue ones only tiny campground wells. That is not what came back.
results.boring: Partial surveys logged under another code: ruled out in part. Counting SNSP and SNSF drops LA DWP (3.9M people) and 3 others, and 117 are left. Outstanding-performer 5-year schedule: ruled out, because the 117 are past even 5 years. Late state uploads: NOT ruled out. NJ big systems show 2022-2025 investigation and records visits (INVG, RSCH), so surveys may be logged under other codes: NOT ruled out. Next step is to ask NJDEP and CA's Division of Drinking Water.
traps: Sanitary surveys come in three codes: SNSV full, SNSP partial, SNSF follow-up. Counting SNSV alone flags LA DWP as unsurveyed since 2017, but it has a partial survey dated 2025-09.
Grade S (significant deficiency) is common: 34% of surveyed community systems got one since 2016, so 'keeps getting S' is weak.
VISIT_DATE holds 1,290 dates before 1950 (1900 placeholders).

results.headline: The triage angle (missed lead-pipe inventory or PFAS deadlines) is dead. The live thread is the LALE rows, Tier 1 lead notices. 288 systems have one (1.195M people), and 96% of them are confirmed by lead test results over 0.015 mg/L. Illinois leads with 38 systems and 803K people: Aurora, Peoria, Elgin. Counting from lead tests directly, 1,029 systems have tested over the lead action level since 2024-10-16, serving 3.27M people.
results.checked: Joined each system's milestone codes to the active roster by state. LSLI and PFAS coverage turned out all or nothing by state. Then joined the LALE rows to the lead-and-copper samples table (PB90 over 0.015 mg/L, sampling periods ending on or after 2024-10-16) and to the roster for people served.
results.hit_means: A named, checked list of systems that tested over the federal lead limit under the new rule, led by an Illinois suburban cluster, with 3.27M people across 1,029 systems.
results.miss_means: LALE rows that don't match lead results would have made them schedule noise. They matched: 276 of 288.
results.boring: The 2024 rule now samples homes with lead pipes, so exceedances climb where lead pipes are (IL has the most): a rule change, not necessarily worse water. NOT ruled out. The 753 over-limit systems with no LALE row are absence, and 393 of them sit in states that never log LALE, so they are not a finding.
traps: LSLI rows are all or nothing by state: 15 oversight agencies (PA, FL, OH, WA, MA, MN, CO and others) have zero. A missing row means a missing upload.
EVENT_ACTUAL_DATE on LSLI and PFAS rows is a due date, not a done date. PFAS dates run 2027-04-26 to 2028-12-31, so nothing is past due.
An LSLI row is a schedule, not proof the inventory was submitted.

results.headline: 'Decades in violation' is an unclosed old violation. In all 2,513 runs of 10 years or more, the last flagged month is the month a return-to-compliance date lands, or the month just before. 44% of those runs went 10+ years with no new violation found, and only 2 sites are in a 10-year-plus run today. The small leftover story is a 2025-26 close-out of 30-year-old violations: 64 runs, 32 of them over 20 years.
results.checked: Found each site's unbroken runs of VIO_FLAG=Y months. For every run of 10 years or more, checked the site's violation records for when each violation was found and when it got a return-to-compliance date. The top 25 were also joined to the facility table for names and to the inspection table for visits.
results.hit_means: States left 1980s-90s hazardous-waste violations open for 20-40 years and then closed them in bulk. That is a records-upkeep story. Reserve Environmental Services, Ashtabula OH (517 months, 125 violations, the last found 2019) is the one long run that looks like a real repeat violator.
results.miss_means: Sites polluting continuously for decades. Almost none: the long runs mostly rest on one violation found decades ago.
results.boring: 'The flag carries forward until someone keys a return-to-compliance date': CONFIRMED, 2,513 of 2,513.
traps: The table only holds months a site was in violation or a serious violator. All 106,419 VIO_FLAG=N rows have SNC_FLAG=Y, so '96% Y' is built in.
A run of Y months measures an unclosed violation record, not ongoing pollution. Example: Indian Refining IL, 1 violation found 1991, 1 inspection ever, flagged until 2025-05.

results.headline: Real but known. Midland TX used 131.4B gallons of frack water, then Lea NM 116.8B, Martin TX 116.1B, Weld CO 112.6B, Eddy NM 107.5B and Reeves TX 101.6B. Permian operators on form v4 all sit within 0.74x to 1.46x of the 21.0M-gallon basin median (SM Energy is highest), so there is no outlier company. Median water per job rose from 1.58M gallons (form v1) to 19.3M (form v4).
results.checked: Summed base water by county, dropping the 28 jobs over 100M gallons as likely typos. Compared operators to their basin peers using Permian v4 jobs only, so the era lines up (17,206 jobs). Joined the water source table on DISCLOSURE_ID to split fresh from produced water.
results.hit_means: The Permian counties each used 100B+ gallons, and Midland alone is 5.9% of all frack water on file. That is widely reported already.
results.miss_means: A single operator using far more water than its basin peers. There isn't one, and water per job is set by basin and era.
results.boring: 'Water per well grows with lateral length': CONFIRMED as the whole shape. The TVD leaders are typos (max 1.2B ft).
traps: There is no date column: job start and end dates are empty, and _SRC_FILE is one file. FF_VERSION (1 to 4) is the only era stand-in.
TOTAL_BASE_WATER_VOLUME is filled on only 31% of v1 rows.
The water source table covers 20,302 of 248,835 disclosures (8.2%), so the fresh-water angle only works on that slice.
Operator names drift: OCCIDENTAL, OXYROCK and COG (now ConocoPhillips) are separate rows, so sums undercount parent companies.

results.headline: The angle misses. Private-owned systems had FEWER health-based violations since 2021 than local-government systems, in every size band (10K-100K people: 9.9% vs 17.8%; 100K+: 12.3% vs 15.4%). Private community systems serve 37.6M of 331M people (11%). The table is a good denominator: every lead-join system matched it.
results.checked: Active community systems by owner type (P private, L local government) within five size bands. Joined to the violations table, aggregated first: distinct health-based violation IDs per system with the compliance period starting 2021-01-01 or later. Also counted wholesaler population.
results.hit_means: Private for-profit systems break health rules more than public ones of the same size. Not found.
results.miss_means: What came back: private systems do better in every band, so there is no ownership story here.
results.boring: Big private systems are investor-owned utilities with paid staff. That fits and wasn't tested further. Wholesaler double counting is confirmed: 2,485 active wholesaler community systems carry 56.6M of the 331M people.
traps: POPULATION_SERVED_COUNT double counts through wholesalers (56.6M of 331M in active community systems). Drop IS_WHOLESALER_IND='Y' before any per-person rate.
Most rows are inactive: 262,883 of 434,040.

results.headline: The #1 buyer of strong oxycodone among 84,334 US pharmacies, 2006-12, was Food City Pharmacy #674 in Knoxville TN, not a Florida pill mill. It bought 13.8M pills of 30mg or more, 64% of its pills. Tennessee runs 8% and its own chain 4.7%. Data match, not verified.
results.checked: Kept TRANSACTION_CODE='S' and rolled pills up by buyer and year in the warehouse (615K rows). Dropped the 2 VA mail-order pharmacies. First tried the posed angle: pills per county resident per pharmacy, outside WV/KY/OH. Then scored each pharmacy on its share of oxycodone 30mg+ pills against its own state and its own chain. Pulled the product mix and the distributor split for the outliers. Outlier set: 160 pharmacies with 40%+ strong oxycodone, 5x+ their state's median volume and 1M+ pills.
results.hit_means: #674 moved 21.6M pills, 19.7x the median Tennessee pharmacy. It took 31.5% of Knox County's 43.9M strong oxycodone pills across 141 pharmacies. The product is immediate-release 30mg tablets. AmerisourceBergen shipped 95.8% of its strong oxycodone. Same profile outside Florida: Lam's Las Vegas (43.6% vs NV 8.6%), Hometown New Castle PA (65.7% vs 8.5%), Briargrove Houston (55.9% vs TX 1.9%). Among the 160 outliers, H.D. Smith supplied 21.1% of the strong oxycodone vs 4.7% nationally (4.5x). River City Pharma was 5.2x and KeySource 4.8x. McKesson was 0.38x and Cardinal 0.43x.
results.miss_means: The per-capita angle as posed is a denominator artifact. Norton VA, a city of 3,687, shows 137 pills per resident per year. The two VA mail-order pharmacies show 184 and 179. A one-year buyer in Kimball NE shows 167. If the strong-oxycodone list had been only Florida and Kermit, it would repeat the 2019 Washington Post story.
results.boring: Pain or cancer pharmacy: only partly ruled out. The mix is immediate-release 30mg, not long-acting cancer doses, but ARCOS has no street address. Public since 2019: NOT ruled out. The Post's pharmacy lookup has been online since 2019, so Knoxville press or a DEA or Tennessee pharmacy board action may already exist. That is the next check. The small-distributor lift is largely known from DEA actions around 2011-12. The QUANTITY angle is dead: RW0294493 is Walgreens' own distribution center, and QUANTITY counts packages.
traps: Per-capita by pharmacy is ruled by tiny county lines: independent cities like Norton VA (3,687 people) and one-year buyers top the list
Connecticut buyers fail the DIM_COUNTY join (2022 planning regions): 675M pills get no population
BUYER_ZIP lost leading zeros in the roll-up sample (NJ 7052)

results.headline: 30-day notices rose from 19% of high-risk device changes in 2000-04 to 64% from 2010 on. Medtronic ICD P980016 has 928 changes, 621 of them 30-day notices. The recall join is dead, and the MAUDE deaths follow how sick the patients are.
results.checked: 1,743 PMAs and 55,380 supplements. Counted the 30-day notice share by 5-year span and by applicant. Searched the recall text for P plus six digits and checked that the firm name agrees. Joined MAUDE death and injury reports by product code.
results.hit_means: MAUDE lands 99.3% of reports on a 510(k) or PMA product code. Codes found only in PMA hold 10,778 of 14,987 death reports (72%). Top: heart pumps (DSQ) 3,033, catheter aortic valves (NPT) 1,136, wearable defibrillators 617. Applicant peers on 30-day share: Medtronic 74%, Boston Scientific 71%, Abbott 60%, Biotronik 46%.
results.miss_means: Only 13 recall rows (12 events, 2 Class I) name a PMA number that lands with the firm agreeing, so recalls can't be tied to the 30-day path. The deaths belong to the sickest patients' devices, not to a review track.
results.boring: Long-lived pacemaker and defibrillator lines pile up manufacturing changes. It's a known research theme. Not ruled out.
traps: HEALTH__FED_FDA_MAUDE runs 2020-01-01 to 2021-09-30 only, and BASELINE_510K_NUMBER is blank on every row
The device recall table has no PMA or product code key, so device-level recall joins fail

results.headline: 442 Class I drug recall events since 2016, and no firm has more than 9. Sterile injectable makers run 33-35% Class I (Fresenius Kabi 9 of 27, AuroMedics 8 of 23) against 12.9% for all firms. That pattern is known.
results.checked: 17,876 rows = 4,643 events, one firm per event. Counted distinct EVENT_ID per firm since 2016, Class I share against all firms, and reason groups. Tried to pull the plant out of the 'Manufactured by' text.
results.hit_means: Firms with 3+ Class I events: 18, holding 76 of the 442 (17%). Class I reasons: sterility or contamination 182, undeclared drugs in supplements 93, label mix-ups 82. All 442 were voluntary. AuroMedics' Class I reasons include glass, mold and rubber in vials.
results.miss_means: No single maker or plant stands far above its peers. The plant text parses on only 25.6% of rows. The Medicare/VA join isn't possible: no warehouse table lists VA or Medicare purchases by maker. A recall pulls lots, not the whole NDC, so 'still sold' is the expected answer anyway.
results.boring: Injectable makers make more sterile products, and one bad vial is a Class I recall. Ruled in.
traps: Rows are recalled products, not recalls: 17,876 rows = 4,643 events
MANUFACTURER_NAME_LIST, PRODUCT_NDC_LIST and APPLICATION_NUMBER_LIST are each filled on about 18% of rows

results.headline: The join the angle needs doesn't exist. The device recall table's K_NUMBER_LIST and PRODUCT_CODE are blank on all 39,635 rows, and the 510(k) table has no predicate column.
results.checked: Profiled HEALTH__FED_FDA_DEVICE_ENFORCEMENT's key fields. Pulled every K plus six digits from the recall description and lot text, joined them to K_NUMBER, and checked that the applicant agrees with the recalling firm. Fallback: a firm-name join, Class I events since 2012 per clearance since 2002.
results.hit_means: Only 132 recall rows (65 events, 7 Class I rows) carry a real K-number with the firm agreeing: 0.3% of rows. On the firm fallback, 87.9% of recall events land on a 510(k) applicant. Highest Class I per clearance: Datascope 14 on 23, Arrow 11 on 22, Hamilton Medical 10 on 31, Smiths Medical 25 on 87, Baxter 32 on 118. The median firm has 0.
results.miss_means: You can't tie a Class I recall to a specific clearance or its predicate here. The firm list is balloon pumps, infusion pumps and ventilators: life-support machines known for recalls.
results.boring: Device type drives Class I, and the big makers have long public recall histories. Not ruled out.
traps: HEALTH__FED_FDA_DEVICE_ENFORCEMENT K_NUMBER_LIST and PRODUCT_CODE are blank on all 39,635 rows
K plus six digits in recall text are mostly lot numbers: one row holds 98,292 matches

results.headline: Talc powder reports hold 26,490 of 26,542 death reports (99.8%). The deaths are J&J talc lawsuits. The table holds cosmetics only, no foods or supplements.
results.checked: Pulled all 85,511 reports and unpacked the PRODUCTS JSON (suspect role). Counted death and hospital outcomes per product by year and report type. Split talc from non-talc, and searched for supplement and food products.
results.hit_means: Talc touches 71,583 reports (83.7%) and 95.6% of hospital stays. Top: 'Johnsons powder no UPC' 13,820 death reports, 'J and J baby powder' 11,186. The MoCRA jump is 25,142 expedited reports in 2024, up from 158 in 2023.
results.miss_means: Outside talc there are 13,928 reports, 52 deaths in 25 years and 725 hospital stays (38 in 2023, 79 in 2024). No product has more than 5 serious reports except SkinShift Vitamin C Serum's 17, all received 2016-03-01 as 'Adverse Reaction': a batch entry. Kratom, energy drinks and Hydroxycut: 0 reports.
results.boring: Lawsuit filings drive the reports. Confirmed, not just named.
traps: CAERS here is cosmetics only; the catalog summary says foods and supplements too
84% of reports and 99.8% of death reports are talc litigation filings
PRODUCT_BRAND_NAME, PRODUCT_INDUSTRY_* and PRIMARY_REACTION_TEXT are empty; products sit in PRODUCTS JSON

results.headline: 64 nonprofits spent $940M in federal money in years after the IRS pulled their exemption, with no reinstatement and not in today's master file. 27 are HUD elderly or disabled housing ($435M), and 5 still hold active HUD Section 202 rent contracts.
results.checked: 1,207,295 rows, 1,187,976 EINs, all 9 digits. Joined EIN to FAC single audits, keeping fiscal years that start after revocation with no reinstatement before year end. Non-profit auditees: 207 of 37,503 EINs (0.55%), $3.40B. 116 of the 207 are in the current IRS master file, so they were reinstated. That leaves 64 EINs, $939.8M, where the name agrees and the EIN isn't in either master file. By name: housing 27 ($434.8M), government 14 ($304.3M), Puerto Rico 8, charter schools 9, credit unions 2, other 4. Second join, HUD Section 8 contracts by name: 6 of 27 housing names land (22%), 5 of them on active 202 contracts: Camellia Manor, Jaycee Estates, Hoover Seniors, Hillside Gulfport Manor, Tupqich Elder Apts. Third join, PPP $150K+ by name and ZIP: 25 clean nonprofit loans, $31.2M, of 56,850 (0.04%).
results.hit_means: HUD elderly-housing money kept going to owner nonprofits that lost their federal tax exemption years ago, and a few still hold active HUD rent contracts.
results.miss_means: If HUD's 202/811 rules don't require IRS exemption, or the IRS reinstated them without the file showing it, this is paperwork, not a story.
results.boring: The revocation file misses reinstatements. The master-file check catches most of those, but not a group that was reinstated and later dissolved. FAC counts the HUD 202 loan balance as federal money every year, so summing across years inflates the dollars. Use the max single year: Hoover $5.36M, Jaycee $3.75M. Governments, Puerto Rico co-ops and credit unions don't need exemption, so they're dropped. Group-exemption members could look revoked; not ruled out. The HUD rule itself is not checked yet.
traps: A blank REINSTATEMENT_DATE does not mean still revoked: 29,792 of 1,011,649 no-reinstatement EINs are in today's IRS master file, 21,110 with a ruling month after the revocation
FAC entity_type 'non-profit' includes government bodies (Hawaii Health Systems Corp, Des Moines schools, UNC Hospitals)
FAC federal-expended for HUD 202 repeats the loan balance every year, so never sum across years

results.headline: Two defect probes have sat open 7-8 years with no recall while complaints kept coming: Nissan false emergency braking PE19010 (2,572 days, 75 complaints before, 273 after) and VW air-bag clockspring EA18003 (3,081 days, 1,413 before, 714 after). The median probe closes in 234 days.
results.checked: 154,380 rows = 5,348 probes. PE/EA probes opened 2010 on: 530, 485 closed, 53.4% with a recall, median 234 days. Folding in the 91 PEs upgraded to EAs gives 60.4%. Per-maker shares run from Hyundai 80% (12/15) to Tesla 40% (4/10); counts are too small to rank makers. Listed still-open probes over 2 years old. Joined complaints on make/model/year and component, before and after the open date. Checked the open flag by decade.
results.hit_means: A preliminary evaluation, meant to be a short first step, has sat 7 years on phantom braking while matching complaints kept arriving. It is the oldest open braking probe by 4.6 years and 11x the median.
results.miss_means: If nhtsa.gov shows PE19010 or EA18003 closed, the file is stale and there is nothing.
results.boring: The file could be stale on these two (not ruled out; check nhtsa.gov). Takata and ARC megaprobes are kept open on purpose and are left out. Press about a probe can drive complaints (not ruled out). The before and after windows differ in length, so these are counts, not rates. Tesla's low raw recall share was an artifact: 5 of its 15 closed probes were upgrades.
traps: Rows are exploded by make/model/year and recall number; dedupe to NHTSA_ACTION_NUMBER
A PE upgraded to an EA reads as 'closed, no recall': 91 of 485 closed probes since 2010
39 pre-2010 probes show open with no close date, and 108 have no open date (107 open): the open flag is only kept up for recent probes
MODEL_YEAR is a float (2012.0)

results.headline: 61 of 22,112 US person names (0.28%) match an SEC insider with the city agreeing. Mostly US executives on the boards of their own companies' Malta subsidiaries.
results.checked: 771,315 rows, one per node. 31,666 tagged USA. After dropping company-looking names: 23,972 person nodes, 22,112 keys (last name + first name). Matched to SEC insider owners (119,889 keys): 828 match (3.7%), 546 map to one CIK, and middle initials agree on 105 and conflict on 197. Second field: the SEC city appears in the ICIJ registered address for 83 keys. Strong matches: 61. Top: Vrattos 20 entities and Bonanno 18 (same NY office, both NextDecade 10% owners). Also Lutnick and Laffer, 1 Malta entity each.
results.hit_means: A US-listed insider has a documented offshore role, a lead for disclosure checks person by person.
results.miss_means: Zero strong matches would mean the join is broken. It works, but it finds ordinary corporate subsidiaries.
results.boring: The Paradise Papers Malta registry is a public company register, and sitting on a subsidiary board is normal. ICIJ already searched and published US names. Being in the leaks is not wrongdoing. Not ruled out for any one name.
traps: 197 of 546 single-CIK name matches have conflicting middle initials: a last+first match is not a person match
86,403 rows are bearer placeholders (THE BEARER, EL PORTADOR), not people

results.headline: A join table with no story of its own. It holds the officer addresses that made the SEC city check possible. The top US intermediaries (Michael B. Edge 448 entities, Westglobe 397) are ICIJ's own 2013/2016 reporting.
results.checked: 3,339,267 rows, 2,901,722 distinct links (13% repeats). officer_of: 1,720,357 rows, 1,291,429 distinct (25% repeats). START_DATE runs 0003 to 5015. 23,550 of 23,972 US person nodes have a registered address through it. Ranked US-address intermediaries by distinct entities.
results.hit_means: A US intermediary nobody has written about would be a lead.
results.miss_means: The top of the list is exactly what ICIJ published, and that is what came back.
results.boring: Already published. Ruled in, not out.
traps: The same link repeats across leaks: count DISTINCT start, end, rel_type
START_DATE holds junk years like 0003 and 5015, and 1969-12-31 as a stand-in

results.headline: Mislabeled: these are ongoing PBGC-insured plans, not failed ones. The top is GM hourly at 322,604 people, still running, and only 13 of 20,835 EINs are in the real trusteed list.
results.checked: 21,596 plans, median 11 participants. The top 15 are GM, AT&T, RTX, UPS, FedEx, Kaiser, JPMorgan and others, all ongoing. 51% are cash balance plans and 59% took effect in 2015 or later. EINs padded and matched to LABOR__FED_PBGC_TRUSTEED_PLANS: 13 overlap, including Delta (pilots' plan dumped in 2006, still 145,914 people in 5 insured plans) and Avaya. Redirected the angle to the real table joined to Form 5500 on SPONS_DFE_EIN: 17 of 5,176 sponsors still file, but the mart is only 33,484 filings.
results.hit_means: A known plan dumper that still sponsors insured plans. Only Delta and Avaya, both known.
results.miss_means: This table can't say who dumped a pension. It lists ongoing insured plans.
results.boring: The famous dumps (Bethlehem 92,174, LTV 63,757, Sears, Pan Am, Delphi, United, US Airways) are in the other table and well covered. The Form 5500 slice is too thin to say any sponsor is gone.
traps: The table name and catalog summary say 'trusteed', but the contents are ongoing insured plans. Use LABOR__FED_PBGC_TRUSTEED_PLANS for failed plans
Form 5500 mart: SPONSOR_DFE_EIN is 100% empty too, not just EIN. SPONS_DFE_EIN is the filled one. PLAN_YEAR_BEGIN_DATE and FORM_YEAR are empty
The fact line's 'top EIN 391K' is UPS's two plans combined

results.headline: Current US company IDs refuse to name the ultimate owner at 5.0% (6,721 of 134,287), second only to Hong Kong and level with the BVI. 91% of those sit with one registrar, Bloomberg: 5.7% on Bloomberg's US book vs 2.3% at every other registrar's US book. Outside the US, Bloomberg matches its peers (UK 1.69% vs 1.69%).
results.checked: Joined REPEX ultimate-parent rows (one per LEI) to GLEIF on LEI. 99.1% land (3,142,422 of 3,169,671). Refusal share = NON_PUBLIC plus the 5 newer refusal codes, divided by every LEI in the group. Ran it by country on all records, then on current (ISSUED) records only. Split US and 9 peer countries by Bloomberg vs other registrars. Grouped US refusals by first address line. Pulled LEI-shaped IDs from OpenSanctions companies: 1,390 sanctioned, 1,246 land in GLEIF, first-5-letter name agreement 57% (Cyrillic names drag that down).
results.hit_means: One registrar's US book lets companies skip naming their owner at 2.5x the rate of every other US registrar. That's a process story about who checks the exception. The 6,721 are live records: all renewed in 2025-26, 3,953 are Delaware entities, 6,603 marked 'fully corroborated', and every one uses the old catch-all NON_PUBLIC code.
results.miss_means: If the gap is client mix (Bloomberg's US book is swap counterparties and fund vehicles), it's just who shops where. On all records the US reads 11.25%, but 83% of that is lapsed records. The registered-agent addresses (CSC 15.2%, CT Corp 13.1%) sit near the US base, so the shell-address angle is dead. Sanctioned targets refuse at 7.1% vs 3.5% for the whole file, but that's only 72 companies.
results.boring: Client mix at Bloomberg, not ruled out. The UK, Jersey and Singapore splits point toward registrar practice. The next pass compares the same legal form, the same Delaware jurisdiction and the same registration year across registrars. 'Owned by people' (NATURAL_PERSONS) is the normal answer and was never counted as a refusal.
traps: 83% of US refusals sit on non-ISSUED (lapsed or retired) records; filter to ISSUED before ranking countries, or the US looks twice as secretive as it is
Refusals on current records all use the legacy NON_PUBLIC code; the 5 specific codes cover only 1,999 LEIs in total

results.headline: Altamaha EMC's '12 days' is Hurricane Helene. Its own storm-excluded number still reads 17,060 of 17,310 minutes, so the major-event split was never done. Its Georgia neighbors did it: Jefferson 10,320 went to 109.
results.checked: Ranked SAIDI with and without major-event days against state medians (1K+ customers for with, 10K+ for without). Customer-weighted averages for the 6 Helene states vs the rest. 744 of 971 rows have the standard IEEE numbers; 221 report only the utility's own method.
results.hit_means: A utility still high after storm days come out would be chronic neglect. The without-MED top list does have 6 East Texas co-ops in its top 14 (Jasper-Newton 1,512 min, Upshur 1,249).
results.miss_means: 16 of the top 20 with-MED utilities are in GA/NC/SC/FL/TN/VA. Customer-weighted without-MED is 131.9 min there vs 131.6 elsewhere: identical once storms come out. With MED it's 1,471 vs 454. The table holds 2024 only, so nothing can be called chronic.
results.boring: Helene, confirmed. The East Texas cluster likely sits near Beryl's July 2024 path; that's outside knowledge, not checked in the data. Co-ops run longer rural lines: 188 min customer-weighted vs 128 investor-owned vs 90 municipal.
traps: 'Without major events' can still hold a hurricane when a utility skipped the IEEE storm-day split. Altamaha EMC carved out 254 of 17,310 minutes; check with-minus-without before calling anything chronic
One municipal row has without-MED > with-MED (impossible); 2 rows read 0

results.headline: The top of the home-price list is the famous big coastal utilities (SDG&E 43.6c, PG&E 39.6c, Con Ed 35.7c, Mass Electric 33.6c, about 2x their state medians). Against same-owner peers the gap mostly goes away: Mass Electric vs the MA investor-owned median is 33.6c vs 34.4c. Joined to outages, price and reliability show no link (correlation 0.08).
results.checked: Cents per kWh = residential revenue ($K) x 100 / residential MWh, on Part A full-service rows with DATA_TYPE 'O'. results.headline: One partner, Ben Borgers, signed 84 to 165 public-company audits a year in 2019-2023; the median partner signs 1. The SEC shut him down in 2024. results.checked: Operating-company audits only (not funds, not benefit plans), newest version of each filing. I counted distinct companies per lead-partner ID per year. Peers: 33,373 partner-years, median 1, p99 12. The Borgers ID reads 51, 78, 84, 95, 121, 162, 165, 88 for 2017-2024. For his 218 clients from 2023-24, I followed each to its next firm: 135 have no later Form AP, 9 went to Fruci, 9 to Boladale Lawal (Lagos), 7 to Bush & Associates (Las Vegas). In 2024-25, 57 of 7,437 partner-years reached 15+ audits. The one-partner firms among them: Olayinka Oyebola (Lagos) 39, Victor Mokuolu (Houston) 36, Chase Bush 34, Boladale Lawal 34, LAO Professionals (Lagos) 19. Tiny-firm partners with 20+ audits a year: 1-3 a year in 2017-22, 4-5 a year in 2023-25. results.miss_means: These would be normal practices. They aren't: each named firm has one lead partner, against a peer median of 1 audit a year.

The Marcum and Withum spikes of 50-111 in 2020-21 are the SPAC boom: ruled out as a lead. The 135 clients with no later audit could have gone dark, deregistered, or simply not filed yet. results.headline: One Weather Service office, Phoenix, logged 1,345 of the 2,145 US heat deaths (63%) in the storm record for 2018-2023, copied from Maricopa County public health counts. It logged no heat events after June 2024, although it kept filing dust storms and floods. The national heat-death count fell from 557 (2023) to 250 (2024) to 99 (2025). Without Phoenix, the count is flat: 205, 177, 98.
results.checked: Summed direct deaths by event type for 1996-2009 and 2010+. Listed the top places by hazard. Pulled heat deaths per year for the Phoenix office (PSR), Las Vegas (VEF), Texas and California. Read the narratives on Phoenix rows. Looked for any renamed heat event type (none). Listed Phoenix's summer filings of any type for 2023-2025. Aggregated FEMA Individual Assistance by incident code for the disaster-dollars angle.
results.hit_means: Storm Data heat deaths measure which office does the paperwork, not the heat. Heat 'outranks' tornadoes 3,352 to 1,313 (2010-2025) largely because of Phoenix plus Las Vegas (70.6% of 2018-23), and the 2024-25 drop is fake. All of Texas logged 120 heat deaths in six years.
results.miss_means: If heat deaths were spread across offices, the table would be a usable national heat count. They are concentrated in 2 of 123 offices, so it isn't. The FEMA 'dollars follow deaths' angle is unresolved: the incident codes are single letters that need a lookup, so absence of heat aid isn't claimed.
results.boring: Storm Data only counts deaths an office can confirm, and it's known to undercount heat compared with death certificates. Phoenix's late-filing lag for summer 2024 is NOT ruled out. It is not where the load stops: the table runs to 2025-12 and Phoenix filed other types through 2025-11. The 'damage per event grew' angle is dead: the median damaged event fell from $10K to $5K to $3K, a change in how damage is estimated.
traps: Heat deaths are mostly the Phoenix office's paperwork, and Phoenix logged no heat after 2024-06
Heat events are zone-based (CZ_TYPE='Z' on 19,676 of 19,677 Excessive Heat rows since 2010), so county-FIPS joins drop every heat death
The median damage estimate halved over time. That's a change in how it's estimated, not a trend. DAMAGE_PROPERTY is text with K/M/B and blank on 34% of rows
The triage's 'None' top county is TOR_OTHER_CZ_NAME, which is filled only when a tornado crosses into another county

results.headline: At the same sites, state hazardous-waste inspectors in IL, NJ and PA find violations far less often than EPA does. Where EPA found violations (2015-2025), a state inspection of the same site within 2 years also found them 15.5% of the time in IL (41 sites), 28.5% in NJ (87), 34.5% in PA (78) and 49.1% nationally (1,202). WI: 80.8% (55). WA: 88.5% (13).
results.checked: Deduped 24,696 repeated site-date-type-agency groups. Kept full compliance inspections (CEI), 2015-2025, dropping U flags. National hit rate: state 38.9% of 124,556 vs EPA 58.4% of 6,327. Large generators only: 44.3% of 38,858 vs 70.5% of 3,293. Checked the Y/N flag against the RCRA violations table: 99.1% of state Y inspections have a same-agency violation logged within 60 days, 1.2% of N inspections do, so the flag is honest (except TX at 17.3%). Paired each EPA CEI with state CEIs at the same site within 730 days, then within 180 days: 347 EPA-found sites, state also found 44.1% (NJ 18.2% of 33, PA 32.9% of 19, WI 91.7% of 12). Named example sites (Safety-Kleen in 4 states, Clean Earth, Calgon Carbon, Arkema); all data match, not verified.
results.hit_means: State programs differ sharply in what they write up at the same facilities. IL/NJ/PA/NC/MD inspectors pass sites EPA writes up. That's a state enforcement-culture story with named sites and a 5x state-to-state spread.
results.miss_means: If the gap had closed at the same sites, the raw state-vs-EPA gap would just be EPA picking bad actors. It stayed open at both 2-year and 180-day windows.
results.boring: EPA targeting: mostly ruled out by the same-site test. Fixes between visits: narrowed by the 180-day window, not fully ruled out (10-90 sites per state). Joint inspections logged twice (EPA writes it up, state logs N): NOT ruled out, next check is pairs 1-14 days apart. SD's 1.8% looks like a recording habit (EPA's SD rate is also 5.3%).
traps: 24,696 site-date-type-agency groups repeat on 2-29 rows; dedupe before any rate
TX state 'N' inspections have a same-agency violation logged within 60 days 17.3% of the time; TX's flag undercounts (real rate about 62% vs 54.5%)

results.headline: 553 water permits broke effluent limits in 36+ of 40 quarters (2016-2025). 152 got no formal action settled in that time, and 84 never had one. In WV, chronic mines got formal action 25.9% of the time (85 mines) vs 57.6% for chronic sewer plants in the same state (191). 63 chronic WV mines have none.

Kept 20,058 permits with 36+ quarters and built a peer ladder: formal-action share rises from 7.9% (0 violating quarters) to 72.5% (36-40). Blank-dated formal actions explain only 4 of 152. Operator roll-up: Magnolia Water (LA) is 85% chronic vs 80.7% for LA municipal plants, so in line. National Water Infrastructure LLC (216 LA permits): violating-quarter share rose from 28% (2016-23) to 82% (2024-25). Its $43.9M in penalties is one $357K order repeated on 123 permits. Named: Sugartree Surface Mine WV (1,373 violations, no formal action ever, no informal 2016-25), Westridge Mine WV (744), Madison Mine MO (744), Campbell Soup Napoleon OH (625), PREPA San Juan (465). All data match, not verified.
