results.miss_means: If the no-action permits had been pending orders or dead permits, there'd be nothing. Checked: 4 of 152 blank-dated, and all 553 report 36+ quarters.
results.boring: State orders that never reach ICIS: NOT ruled out. WV reports zero informal actions to ICIS for every permit kind, so WV mine enforcement may live in a state mining system. Next check is WV DEP's own list. Pre-2016 consent decrees covering mines: not checked. Small-village affordability explains the AK/IL/OH sewer entries, not mines or Campbell Soup. NWI's 2024 jump could be new limits or new monitoring: not ruled out.
traps: WV reports zero informal actions to ICIS 2016-2025 for every permit kind; 'no action' in WV means 'no formal action on record'
NPDES formal enforcement actions repeat one case's penalty on every permit it covers: LA-SAWE180039 $357,000 x 123 permits reads as $43.9M; sum by ENF_IDENTIFIER first
Confirms R-286: HLRNC 'S' quarters carry a violation count only 39% of the time; quarters before 1996 and after 2026Q3 exist only when violating

results.headline: The top 25 is all GA and FL sewer overflows. DeKalb County's Snapfinger Creek plant logged 1,394 overflows since Oct 2016 against $52,344 in formal-action penalties since 2015 (about $38 per overflow), and hit its high of 202 in 2025. Known consent-decree story. The national ranking just maps which states report.
results.checked: 305,445 rows. Since 2015: 230,540 rows, 229,356 distinct permit+date+code (0.5% dups). Overflow codes: 28,033 events. Top permits with names (99.99% land) and formal actions since 2015: DeKalb 1,394 overflows, 4 actions, $52,344. Atlanta 1,114, 8 actions, $1,425,924. Cobb 438. Tampa 356. Overflows by year: national 371 (2016) to 3,731 (2025), only 21-36 states report any. FL 0 before 2018, 1,278 in 2024. DeKalb 131-176 a year from 2018 to 2024, then 202 in 2025. Atlanta fell from 208 to 84.
results.hit_means: DeKalb's overflows rose in 2025 while it's under a federal decree, with tiny penalty dollars in this system. A local story.
results.miss_means: National worst-spiller lists are dead: counts track reporting regimes, not spills.
results.boring: Size and reporting drive counts (confirmed). Decree-stipulated penalties may be paid outside this table or before 2015 (not checked). No gallons column.
traps: Overflow counts map which states report: FL went from 0 before 2018 to 1,000+ a year; only 21-36 states report any
US MCAS Cherry Point NCL003816: 219 rows collapse to 6 distinct date-code events
Top code D0017 is a catch-all ('violation specified in comment')

results.headline: Of 38,091 distinct enforcement-order milestones, 6,567 (17%) were never met, but only 1,377 are real construction or compliance work, and the max per permit is 11 (Binghamton-Johnson City STP, NY). The triage 'Tennessee leads' angle is fake: it summed a sequence number, and TN holds 1.3% of rows.
results.checked: Counted distinct COMP_SCHEDULE_EVENT_ID (one milestone sits on up to 4 rows). 100% of 10,589 permits land in facilities and formal actions. 7,771 are still reporting in 2025+ and hold 5,901 unmet milestones (1,163 work). Top: Binghamton-Johnson City 11 work milestones (oldest 2005). Wingo STP KY 13 unmet (6 work) since 1989, 17 effluent-violation quarters in 2021-25. Pay-civil-penalty milestones never marked paid: 442 of 2,295. Checked by state: VI 61 of 65, LA 116, MS 50, which track each state's general habit of leaving milestones open. LA/TX/AR/OK hold 61% of rows.
results.hit_means: A live permit with a decades-old unmet construction order and current effluent violations (Wingo KY) is a small local story.
results.miss_means: No big 'missed court deadlines for decades' pattern: max 11 per permit, mostly small-town sewer plants.
results.boring: Milestones never closed out in the system after the order ended: not ruled out, likely. The unpaid-penalty rate tracks state data-entry habit (VI leaves 78.9% of everything open). No dollar amounts in CS.
traps: COMP_SCHEDULE_NMBR is a schedule sequence number up to 999; the triage TN0025011 '35.9K' was its sum
One milestone sits on up to 4 violation rows (11,787 event IDs x4); count distinct COMP_SCHEDULE_EVENT_ID
LA/TX/AR/OK (EPA Region 6) hold 61% of rows: data-entry practice, not a violation map

results.headline: It's a table of late paperwork. Of 41,769 never-met permit deadlines due 2016 to mid-2025, 98.4% are certifications, applications and reports. Real work: 653 across 433 live permits, max 7 (Suncor Commerce City refinery, oldest due Oct 2024).
results.checked: Counted 189,289 distinct PERM_SCHEDULE_EVENT_ID (63,338 sit on 4 rows each). Milestones due 2016-2025H1 with a violation: 97,436. Never met: 41,769, of which 41,116 are paperwork (annual inspection certification 8,642, permit application 4,901, monitoring report 4,597) and 653 are work by keyword match. Ranked live permits by unmet work milestones with names.
results.hit_means: Nothing big. At most a Suncor refinery footnote, which is recent and already known.
results.miss_means: Confirmed: the 'decades of missed construction deadlines' angle isn't in this table.
results.boring: Paperwork (confirmed, 98.4% of unmet). Municipal consent-decree slippage isn't even visible here: the top work misses are Colorado gravel pits.
traps: One milestone sits on up to 4 violation rows (63,338 PERM_SCHEDULE_EVENT_IDs x4); count distinct event IDs
A keyword split by 'implement' also catches SWPPP implementation certifications, which are paperwork

results.headline: 157 sanctioned people match a UK company controller (PSC) on full name plus birth year and month. Among matches whose company is in the Companies House table, 45 people still control 83 active UK companies: 21 OFAC SDN people on 42 companies, 19 UK-sanctioned people on 32. The standout is OFAC transnational-crime designee Ka On Kong, who controls 22 London companies (restaurants, clubs, 'network technology' shells) filed 2022-2025 at 2 shared addresses. Data match, not verified.
results.checked: Join A: sanctioned people with a full birth date (21,670) against UK PSC individuals. Surname token + forename token + birth year + birth month must agree, then full-name equality. Result: 157 people, 309 companies. Then the Companies House table for company status (176 of 332 rows landed). Join B: Organization, Company and LegalEntity names, normalized with legal suffixes stripped and 2+ words, against USAspending contracts R2 recipients (93M rows). Result: 227 matches, but only 28 once the recipient's country must be one of the listed countries, and those got about $1M after first-seen.
results.hit_means: The listed person really is the UK controller. Then a US- or UK-sanctioned drug, terror or organized-crime figure runs a live UK company web, which is barely reported outside the Russian oligarchs.
results.miss_means: It's a same-name, same-birth-month stranger. That's plausible for common names (Muhammad Iqbal, Jian Zhang), weak for Ka On Kong (22 companies, shared addresses, matching nationality). Check Companies House officer pages for the full birth date against the OFAC entry.
results.boring: An asset freeze doesn't dissolve a company, so 'Active' can mean frozen. OFSI licences are not ruled out. The oligarch holdings (Abramovich, Kantor, Potanin) are already covered. In join B the big hits (Lockheed, Booz Allen, General Dynamics) sit on China's and Iran's counter-sanction lists; that noise is ruled out.
traps: OpenSanctions FIRST_SEEN is when OpenSanctions picked up the entry, not the designation date (568 distinct days, bulk days like 2023-04-20). 'Paid after listing' can't be measured from it.
OpenSanctions holds China and Iran counter-sanction lists, so US defense contractors look 'sanctioned'. Filter those lists out.
Suffix-stripped name joins make US look-alikes ('Scott Technologies FZE' UAE vs Scott Technologies Inc US, $320M). Require country agreement.
CORPORATE_REGISTRY__INTL_UK_COMPANIES_HOUSE lacks 47% of the company numbers PSC points to (156 of 332 here, many OE/SL numbers). Blank status is not 'dissolved'.

results.headline: New Mexico cleared 22.3% of homicides in 2022 and 23.2% in 2023, the lowest of all 51 both years. The nation was 56% (2022-23). NM was 47.2% in 2015-19 and 75.1% in 1985-89. Neighbors, 2020-23: AZ 68.7%, CO 73.5%, UT 64.6%, OK 57.9%, TX 57.2%. No reporting gap.
results.checked: Summed homicide offenses and clearances by state and year; rate = clearances / offenses. Flagged years where homicides fell below 70% of the state's own 2015-19 average, and months where violent-crime clearances were under 5% of offenses. NM: 12 months reported every year, homicide counts rising (155, 231, 242, 233), no low-clearance months. Violent-crime clearance 41% to 29% and aggravated assault 48% to 33% (2015 to 2023). The slide starts in 2018 (34%), before NIBRS.
results.hit_means: NM police close under a quarter of homicides: the worst in the country and falling for 6 years. Albuquerque probably drives most of it, but this state-level table can't show agencies.
results.miss_means: NM agencies send clearances to the FBI late or only partly. Then it's a reporting story, not a policing one. Check against agency-level NIBRS data for the Albuquerque police.
results.boring: The national clearance decline is well reported. NIBRS counts clearances differently: only partly ruled out, since the drop predates NIBRS and NIBRS-reporting neighbors didn't collapse (when each state switched was not checked). Late clearances hit every state alike. Agency-level late reporting is not ruled out.
traps: IL clearances aren't reported 2010-2020: 1-3% of violent crime every month, then 22-35% from 2021. Never rank IL on clearance before 2021.
NY clearance jumps from 17% (2010-12) to 63% (2013). NY 2021 has only 232 homicides (NIBRS hole), and NY 2022 violent-crime clearance reads 12%. All reporting artifacts.
MT 1994 is blank on all 10 offenses.

results.headline: Roosevelt Cayman Asset Company filed 1,259 federal foreclosures in Puerto Rico, 2015-2025, all under diversity jurisdiction. That's 31% of PR's 3,711 federal foreclosures under its main spelling alone. 50.2% ended in default judgment, against about 35% for other PR foreclosure plaintiffs and 12.0% in all other districts. Sister shells: Bautista (107), Triangle (20), Abbey (7) Cayman Asset Company. Data match, not verified.
results.checked: Kept one row per case (10,857,396 rows; 41,465 repeat across yearly files). Filings since 2015 grouped by plaintiff: cases, main NOS code, disposition shares (12 voluntary dismissal, 13 settled, 4 default; codes from memory of the FJC codebook, not checked), open share, median days to close. Then NOS 220 foreclosures in PR (district 04) vs all other districts. Then every plaintiff with 'CAYMAN' in the name. Known serial filers confirmed: Strike 3 Holdings, 21,600 copyright suits since 2017, 82% voluntarily dismissed; Malibu Media 4,556; Joe Hand 1,434.
results.hit_means: One offshore loan-pool vehicle turned PR federal court into a foreclosure lane: a third of the island's federal foreclosures, half won by default.
results.miss_means: It's just the biggest holder of distressed PR mortgages, and PR borrowers don't answer suits whoever sues. The test is 50% vs the ~35% for PR peers, not vs the mainland's 12%. Pull a sample of PACER dockets: are the defaults real or statistical closings, and who is the sponsor?
results.boring: The Cayman registration is exactly what creates diversity jurisdiction, which is legal and ordinary. These are likely bought pools of failed-bank loans (not verified). Ruled out: that the default rate is only an island-wide effect (about 15 points over PR peers). Not ruled out: loan mix. The serial-plaintiff angle (Strike 3, Malibu, Joe Hand) is real but already well known.
traps: Civil rows repeat across the yearly files, including the 2099 pending file (41,465 extra rows). Dedupe on district + office + docket + file date before counting cases.
PLAINTIFF is a surname for people (JOHNSON, SMITH top the list) and splits one filer across spellings (STRIKE 3 HOLDINGS, LLC vs STRIKE 3 HOLDINGS LLC; ROOSEVELT CAYMAN ASSET COMANY).

results.headline: 2 dockets were assigned to a judge while the judge's spouse drew director fees from the defendant. Liotti v. Jet Blue Airways (SDNY 1:17-cv-00838, closed in 5 days; Judge Colleen McMahon, spouse JetBlue director fees 2014-18). Gardner v. Procter & Gamble Fed. Inc (NDIL 1:09-cv-06690; Judge Harry Leinenweber, spouse P&G director fees 2004-09). The broader employer pass found 11 in-window pairs out of 1,008. Data match, not verified.
results.checked: 20,174 lines on 13,530 reports, years 2003-2020 (not 2021-23). Joined through FINANCIAL_DISCLOSURES to JUDGES: 88% land, 2,239 judges. Pass 1: 1,008 judge-employer pairs (587 judges) searched against the CourtListener dockets assigned to that judge (504 judges, 4.9M dockets) for case names holding the employer. 32 pairs hit, 11 within disclosure years ±1, about 5 plausible (the biggest: Judge Sheri Chappell, 5 Lee Memorial cases). Pass 2: 956 director, board or trustee lines at 148 judges; 51 company names at 20 judges; 23 hits, 3 in window, 1 false (Panasonic contains SONIC CORP).
results.hit_means: A spouse who is a director of a party means mandatory recusal under 28 USC 455(b)(5)(i). If the judge ruled, that's a story.
results.miss_means: The judge recused and the case was reassigned, or it was dismissed on intake. The 5-day and 3-month closes fit that, and CourtListener's assigned judge can be the first draw. It needs a PACER docket check. 'Fed.' in Gardner may be a P&G credit union, not P&G.
results.boring: CourtListener only holds dockets someone pulled, so land rates are floors. There's no counsel table, so 'the spouse's law firm appears before the judge' can't be tested. 3% of lines are redacted and OCR junk is heavy. Recusal is not ruled out.
traps: DATE_CREATED is CourtListener's 2021-23 load date; the disclosure years (YEAR_COL on FINANCIAL_DISCLOSURES) run 2003-2020.
Substring docket search fires on fragments: 'SONIC CORP' sits inside 'PANASONIC CORP'. Hand-check every hit.

results.headline: 54 of 210 banned people have a same-name, same-state SAM exclusion. 44 are HUD bans, every one dated before the FHFA ban, and 8 are SBA bans on the known Ayvazyan/Dadyan/Terabelian PPP-fraud family. PPP and federal contracts: 0 real hits.
results.checked: People against SAM exclusions (first + last name, state as the second field) and against PPP loans of $150K and up (both name tokens + state). The 31 companies against SAM, PPP, USAspending contracts R2 and HMDA lender names (normalized name equality). Only 82 of 241 bans predate PPP, so 'PPP after the ban' was possible for a third at most. PPP: 1 person hit (Jose L. Garcia DDS, a different city, a collision); 3 company hits, all in other states. Contracts: 0. HMDA: Live Well Financial (collapsed 2019) and First Mortgage Company (Inc vs LLC).
results.hit_means: A banned lender still making mortgages. That can't be tested here: national HMDA after 2017 isn't loaded, only DC samples. Not treated as absence.
results.miss_means: Nothing new. The overlaps are the system working: HUD bans first, FHFA copies.
results.boring: Confirmed: 241 rows of mostly already-convicted people; the SBA overlap is a known federal case; name matching on people is weak.
traps: The FHFA ban list trails HUD. All 46 same-state HUD rows are dated before the FHFA effective date, so overlap with SAM is expected, not a finding.

results.headline: In ICIS-Air, Nebraska shows zero state formal air enforcement actions every year from 2017 to 2025 (it filed 4-26 a year in 2000-14). It resolved 4 of 58 high-priority violations since 2015 (6.9%); the state median is 79%. 13 of 120 operating majors (10.8%) sat in Unaddressed HPV status for all 12 quarters, all with zero formal actions; the state median is 0.4%. 9 of the 13 are ethanol, corn or soy plants (Green Plains, KAAPA, POET, ADM Columbus, AGP Hastings and others). Data match, not verified.
results.checked: Pulled every active ECHO facility whose 3-year history reads S (significant violation) in at least 11 of 12 quarters: 5,619 facilities, 4,415 with FORMAL_ACTION_COUNT = 0. Split them by program. Joined ICIS-Air CURRENT_HPV by registry ID as a second field; it agrees on 200 of 210 air-only facilities. Kept 12-of-12 S plus Unaddressed: 261 facilities. Rated per operating major by state. Then a state roll-up of ICIS-Air formal actions, HPVs resolved and HPVs open 3+ years since 2015, and formal actions by year from 2000 to 2025.
results.hit_means: Nebraska's air regulator either stopped formal enforcement or stopped reporting it to EPA, which is required for HPVs at majors. Either one is a state-enforcement and EPA-oversight story. It stands out on three separate per-major measures.
results.miss_means: Nebraska would look like its peers once you divide by majors. It doesn't: 0.04 state formal actions per major against a 0.79 median; 29.2 open-3yr HPVs per 100 majors against 1.35.
results.boring: NDEE may settle cases by consent orders or letters that never get keyed into ICIS-Air. Not ruled out. Nebraska still logs 53-69 full evaluations of majors a year and 668 informal actions, so the data flow is alive. A records request for NDEE air consent orders 2017-2025 settles it. The ECHO penalty angle is known national settlements (BP $3.37B, VW $1.45B). The 3,360 water-only chronic violators are probably missed discharge reports; that is unverified.
traps: FORMAL_ACTION_COUNT counts only about the last 5 years. Among chronic violators, every row reading 0 has its last formal action on or before 2021-06-18, and 1,328 read 0 with an older DATE_LAST_FORMAL_ACTION on file. 79 of 110 air-only 'zero formal' facilities are ICIS 'Addressed'.
SIGNIFICANT_NONCOMPLIANCE_FLAG is constant 'N' (already known). Use the S letters in THREE_YR_COMPLIANCE_HISTORY instead.

results.headline: 227 Texas operating major air sources still report emissions or show ICIS activity since mid-2021, but have no full compliance evaluation in 5+ years, and no sibling major permit at the site got one either. That is 9.1 per 100 Texas majors against a 1.0 state median. New Mexico is 20.6 (33 of 160). Examples: Praxair Texas City (no FCE ever on record), Performance Materials NA Orange (last FCE 2012), Cemex Balcones (2009), Targa Mont Belvieu (2005). Data match, not verified.
results.checked: Took the last on- or off-site full evaluation (FCE) for each of 13,559 operating majors in the ICIS-Air facility table. Texas: 1,221 of 2,481 (49.2%) are 5+ years stale or never evaluated; the state median is 3.6%. Alive test: any stack test, violation, or informal or formal action since mid-2021, or a TRI, GHG or CAMD emissions report for 2022+. Dropped plants where a sibling major permit at the same registry ID got an FCE. Checked Texas FCE counts per year from 2012 to 2025.
results.hit_means: A named list of running Texas and New Mexico majors not fully evaluated in 5-20 years, at 9-20x the median state. EPA policy expects roughly every 2 years.
results.miss_means: The stale plants would all be dead records. About 79% of Texas's stale majors are, so the raw 49% headline is wrong; only the alive 227 count.
results.boring: TCEQ may log inspections under a minor or area permit at the same site, or in its own system without flowing them to ICIS. Partly ruled out: sibling majors were checked, minors were not. Texas logs about 700 FCEs a year against about 1,500 live majors, so the yearly total is close to policy and the gap sits on specific plants. Next step: check 10 names in TCEQ's CCEDS investigation search.
traps: About 80% of Texas majors with no FCE in 5 years show no activity or emissions since mid-2021. They are dead records still marked OPR.
GHG joined by REGISTRY_ID repeats across sibling permits: Clariant, Celanese and Praxair Clear Lake each show 845,112 t.
25 junk dates before 1970 (years 0025, 0208, 0217).

results.headline: Small lead. 30 of 44 Iowa plants with 3+ failed stack tests since 2015 have no formal action since 2015 (68.2%); the state median is 15.7%. Iowa's fail rate is 9.3% against a 3.5% median. Grain Processing Corp, Muscatine: 53 failed tests out of 220, in 11 separate years 2015-2025, 0 formal actions since 2015, 41 informal actions. Data match, not verified.
results.checked: For each facility with a failed test since 2015 (2,689 facilities, 8,867 fails, 2.9% of pass-plus-fail tests): counted fails, retest passes on the same pollutant within 180 days (53.7% of fail rows), and ICIS-Air formal actions, informal actions and violations since 2015. Every one of the 2,689 lands in the ICIS-Air facility table with a name. Compared the zero-formal share of repeat failers across the 31 states with 5+ of them.
results.hit_means: Iowa lets repeat stack-test failures ride on warning letters (843 informal actions since 2015; state formal actions fell from 9-80 a year in 2000-14 to 1-6 a year). Muscatine is the named case.
results.miss_means: The national angle mostly fails: 104 of 113 plants with 10+ fails drew a formal action since 2015, and 79% of all repeat failers did.
results.boring: Iowa may simply record fails more honestly (Florida logs 0.6%). Or Iowa may treat stack fails as lower-tier violations that a retest clears; it still resolves 41 of 55 HPVs. Not ruled out; pull GPC's Iowa DNR file. This overlaps the Nebraska lead (Nebraska: 8 of 10 repeat failers with no formal action).
traps: One row is one unit x pollutant test, not one test day. San Joaquin Valley logs 100+ in a day; Ampersand Chowchilla has 120 fails on 2021-05-10.
Ohio sent 2 stack-test records since 2015 for 547 majors. A missing stack test is a data gap, not a clean record.
POLLUTANT_DESCS is empty (known). POLLUTANT_CODES is blank on about a third of rows. Dates include years 0201 and 1016.

results.headline: Dow Chemical Louisiana Operations (Plaquemine) reported 34,369 lb of ethylene oxide air release in 2023, 32,106 lb of it fugitive (leaks). That is 8.7x its 2015-22 high and 21% of the 2023 national TRI EtO air total (160,219 lb). It fell back to 2,433 lb in 2024. National TRI EtO fell from 216.8K lb/yr (2015-19) to 149.1K (2022-24). Data match, not verified.
results.checked: Program x year grid: EIS only in 2008, 2011, 2014, 2017, 2020; TRIS 2015-24; E-GGRT 2015-23; CAMD 2015-24. Compared TRI with EIS on the same registry ID, pollutant and year for 2017 and 2020: 36,653 of 80,723 TRI facility-pollutant-years match. Traced EtO by facility and year with ECHO names. Cross-checked the Dow figure and its fugitive/stack split in TRI_BASIC_2023.
results.hit_means: A one-year EtO leak spike at Dow Plaquemine (54% minority neighbors per ECHO), worth one LDEQ incident-records pull.
results.miss_means: The TRI-vs-EIS disagreement angle is dead. The median TRI/EIS ratio is exactly 1.00 for every top pollutant, so EIS reuses TRI; only 7.0% of both-positive pairs differ 10x. EtO did not rise overall.
results.boring: The Dow spike is probably a single upset event already reported to LDEQ; not ruled out. Sterilization Services of Virginia (13,821 lb in 2022, #2 nationally) is probably already on EPA's public EtO lists.
traps: EIS copies TRI for point toxics (median ratio 1.00). It is not an independent second source.
The same Port Neches EtO report (20,180 lb in 2023) sits under registry 110072129444 (named Indorama) here and under FRS 110000599567 (named Huntsman) in TRI_BASIC_2023.
531K zero rows; ANNUAL_EMISSION is text.

results.headline: No environmental-justice gradient within peers. The dirtiest-quarter coal plants have 9.7% minority neighbors against 8.6% for the cleanest quarter; gas runs the other way (20.7% dirtiest vs 32.6% cleanest). The top 'dirtiest per MWh' gas plants are a repowering artifact. The real top is Pennsylvania waste-coal plants, which are already known.
results.checked: Ranked 1,281 plants over 100K MWh by CO2 lb/MWh (medians: coal 2,273, gas 908). Joined eGRID plant ID to the CAMD rows in the combined emissions table, then registry ID, then ECHO PCT_MINORITY. 829 of 1,106 fossil plants have a registry ID and 791 land in ECHO; the state agrees on 791 of 791. Compared CO2-rate quarters within coal and within gas. Looked up the impossible-rate plants by name.
results.hit_means: Dirtier-per-MWh plants would have more minority neighbors than their own fuel peers.
results.miss_means: What happened: coal is flat and gas is inverted. No story on this angle. There is no county income table in the warehouse, so the 'poor counties' half could not run.
results.boring: Big coal plants sit in rural areas. Ruled in. EPA publishes this ranking itself.
traps: Repowered sites carry CO2 twice: the old plant ID has smokestack CO2 and the new ID an EIA estimate. AES Huntington Beach 335 vs 62116, AES Alamitos 315 vs 62115, Lauderdale 613 vs Dania Beach 65978. Impossible rates (31,855 lb/MWh; Alamitos about 51,700 Btu/kWh), up to about 5.3M t counted twice.
Two more impossible gas rates are unexplained (Gleason TN 6,341; Antelope Elk TX 3,419).
Row 1 is a header row (PNAME), and the numeric columns are text.

results.headline: Most of the link churn is URL rewrites, paging and one redesign around Feb 2-4, 2026. Two dated changes are left. The 'Download all files (.zip)' link was on 11 data-set pages; all 11 lost it between Jan 30 and Feb 9, 2026, and none got it back through the last capture in early June. On Feb 21 and Feb 24, 12 court-case links were renamed to '[redacted] v. Indyke/Maxwell/Epstein', hiding plaintiff names that are already in public court records.
results.checked: 24,897 links from 13 pages; the main page was captured 77 times. For each page and link I found the first and last capture it appeared in, and called a link vanished if it was missing from that page's newest capture. I sorted vanished links by kind, checked whether the same link text was still on the page, and searched both Wayback tables for the link after Feb 10. Then I listed every link on the main page's newest capture (2026-05-26).
results.hit_means: DOJ took away a public feature (the bulk zip download) or changed what the public page says (it blacked out plaintiff names in case titles), and the table dates each change to within a few days.
results.miss_means: 516 of the 627 vanished PDF links are the same file under a re-encoded URL. Data set 1 losing 50 files in 3 hours is one page of the listing shifting. The 32 BOP jail-video hour links moved to a /bop-video-footage page. The 16 older PDFs (flight log, contact book, masseuse list, OIG memo, OPR report) probably moved to the new 'First Phase' and 'Memoranda' pages, but this table never captured those pages.
results.boring: Mostly stands. One redesign changed the navigation on all 13 pages at once. The zip removal and the redactions fit a victim-privacy cleanup after the Jan 30 release. The topic is heavily covered, and I did not check news to see whether these two dated changes were already reported.
traps: Diff vanished links on the link text, not the HREF: 516 of 627 'vanished' PDF links are URL-encoding rewrites.
The listing pages capture only page 1 of each data set, so a file dropping off can be paging, not deletion.

results.headline: Against counties of the same size (base population 800 to 40K), the 54 flagged counties got $45 of SAMHSA money per person in FY2019-25, against $92 for counties with the same overdose ranking, $97 for jail-top-only and $93 for the rest. 22% of flagged counties got any SAMHSA money, against 34% of the overdose group. There is no clinic gap: 14.8% have a Medicare methadone clinic, against 15.2%.
results.checked: Two joins. (1) Medicare opioid treatment clinics, matched to counties through the ZIP-to-county table: 1,340 of 1,340 clinics landed on a county. (2) USAspending assistance, SAMHSA only, FY2019-25, summed by the county where the grant is carried out: $50.5B in all, $39.2B carries a county code, and $37.1B (73%) lands on counties in this table. Denominator: base population, worked out as JAIL_POPULATION / JAIL_RATE x 100K. I ran it once on all counties and once size-matched.
results.hit_means: The places jailing people while they die of overdoses get half the federal treatment money per person of same-size counties with the same overdose ranking.
results.miss_means: There is no clinic gap, because small counties rarely have a methadone clinic in any group. Without the size match the money gap is inflated ($45 against $151), so part of the raw gap is just county size.
results.boring: Not ruled out. Most SAMHSA money is block grants booked where the state agency sits. The money arrives in lumps (the median county in every group got $0). KY, TN and VA are 28 of the 54, so how each state routes money could explain the gap. Next step: compare against same-size counties within each state and follow the state subgrants.
traps: JAIL_RATE_YEAR mixes years: 1,405 counties use 2024, 562 use 2023, 549 use 2019, and 78 are older than 2015. Counties from different years are ranked against each other.
Seven SW Virginia counties (Dickenson, Wise, Russell, Norton, Buchanan, Lee, Tazewell) all read JAIL_RATE exactly 1,068: one regional jail copied to seven counties.

The overdose number is a band, and the top band '>30' has no ceiling. JAIL_POPULATION can be fractional (Bristol city VA reads 0.06). KY and UT county jails hold state prisoners (Beaver UT 7,939, Grayson KY 4,404).

results.headline: One clean hit. NAI Logistics B.V. results.headline: One April 2026 report: $79,647.58 of lobbyist-paid transport. A private jet flew 8 people to New York on 2026-03-30/31, including SENATOR Angela Paxton and REPRESENTATIVES Brad Buckley and Caroline Fairly. Clients on the report: Success Academy and Kleinheinz Capital Partners. It's the 3rd-biggest transport total of 3,448 Texas lobby reports with any transport since 1991 (median $188). The state bank commissioner (Charles Cooper) also flew on the bank lobby's private planes in 2016, 2019 and 2022. Data match, not verified against primary records.
results.checked: 3,697 lines, 621 reports, 2004-2026; 111 are private-air lines. The table has no dollar column, so I joined each trip's REPORT_ID to the cover sheet's REPORT_INFO_IDENT for the report's transport dollars, and to TX_LOBBY_INDIVIDUAL_REPORTING for client names. I pulled every line of report 101046715 (Julie Linn Minnehan): all 15 lines are private-air legs, Austin/Fort Worth to New York and back, one night at the NY Hilton Midtown, 'Educational tour and meetings'. Then I ranked all cover reports by transport dollars. #1 is Bionat 2024 at $156K with no itemized lines. #2 is an AIPAC Israel trip in 2011 at $131K. Private-air lines by payer show Cooper (COMMISSNR) flown by IBAT's Williston (15 lines on 3 reports in 2016, 3 lines in 2019), TBA's Sandberg (5 lines in 2016) and Scurlock (1 line in 2022). The AGC of Texas resort trips: Maui 2010 $69.9K, Banff 2007 $67.1K. Also in 2026, the Fermi America site tour for Kelly Hancock and James Dyer, $7.9K.
results.hit_means: A 2026 private-jet trip for a senator and House members, with a charter network and an investment firm as the clients, is the third-costliest Texas lobby travel report in 35 years. A deeper pass asks whether it's been reported, who owned the plane, and what the members carried or voted on afterward. The bank regulator on the regulated industry's planes is a second, smaller clean thread.
results.miss_means: If the $79.6K covered other trips or were a typo, the rank would fall. As far as the table allows, that's ruled out: the report's only transport lines are these 15 legs. Client lines are per report, not per line, so which client paid is not shown.
results.boring: Texas lets lobbyists pay travel and lodging for officials who speak at or attend events, as long as it's reported. This was reported, 'educational tours' are common, and AGC resort conferences have run for decades. Legality is not in question. The size and the client are the news. I didn't check whether the trip was already covered in the press.
traps: TX_LOBBY_TRANSPORTATION has no money column; the dollars exist only per report on TX_LOBBY_COVER.TOTAL_EXPEND_TRANSPORTATION, so a per-official trip cost can't be computed
LODGINGSTREETCOUNTRYCD reads USA for Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Banff; foreign-trip counts from it undercount
Texas client lines (INDIVIDUAL_REPORTING) are per report, not per line; they land on 45% of transport reports and don't exist before 2000
The #1 transport report ever (Christian Bionat, 2024-03, $156,254) has zero itemized lines and no client: either a typo or an unitemized trip, unresolved

results.miss_means: If 'media' meant something else, the number would mislead. It's the lobbyist-reported media and advertising category, on 12 of 12 Abboud reports in 2025.
results.boring: Sands' Texas casino campaign and its ads were covered in the press both sessions. The earlier spikes (TXU 2007, cable franchising 2005) are known fights, and food follows the session calendar. Ruled out: Sands being one of many. Not checked: whether the five-year TEC total is already published.

results.headline: In Oklahoma, veteran suicides went from 228 (2019-20) to 287 (2022-23), a rate of 37.9 to 50.7 per 100K (1.34x). The state's general-population suicide rate stayed flat, 20.4 to 20.3. Kansas shows the same shape: 130 to 160 deaths, 1.35x, against 1.11x for everyone else. Nationally, veteran deaths didn't rise (6,523 in 2013, 6,398 in 2023). The rate rose 20% only because the number of veterans fell from 22.15M to 18.18M.
results.checked: Crude rate per state (deaths / veteran pop), pooled 2011-13 vs 2021-23 and 2019-20 vs 2022-23. Put against the same state's CDC all-suicide rate for the same years, using a fixed panel of counties CDC counted in all four years (the CDC file has no state rows). Then year by year for OK, KS, MT, UT and the nation. OK saw 287 deaths where about 215 were expected at the old rate, about 4.9 SD. KS saw 160 against about 119, about 3.8 SD.
results.hit_means: Something veteran-specific is going on in Oklahoma (and maybe Kansas). It's not the statewide suicide trend, and it's not the shrinking-veteran-population math, because the deaths themselves rose.
results.miss_means: A small-number wobble driven mostly by 2023 (OK: 114, 114, 131, 126, 161) that 2024 data washes out.
results.boring: The VA ranks states yearly and the Mountain West is known. Crude rates with no age adjustment, but ruled out for OK because deaths rose, not just the rate. Not ruled out: the 2023 spike (without it, OK is up about 13%). Also not ruled out: the peer line uses only the 15 OK counties CDC counted all four years (1,089 of 1,292 counted 2019-20 deaths), so suppressed rural counties are missing.
traps: The CDC injury county file has no state rows (GEOID is always 5 digits); state sums drop suppressed counties (1,322 of 3,142 counties counted for suicide in 2019)
VA state file: DC blank all 23 years; VT/DE/RI rates blank 16-20 of 23 years; a 'U.S. Total' row sits in the STATE column

results.checked: LEIE NPI joined to PECOS enrollment, with the file dated 2026-06-29 from ENRLMT_ID. Name-only LEIE businesses and people joined to PECOS on name + state, enrolled after the ban, with middle initial, specialty and NPPES city as second fields. LEIE people joined to NPPES authorized officials on first + last + state + city, then Part B 2024 money. Suffix and namesake-density checks on the best matches. Reused: Part B/D, Open Payments, relief fund and home health owners from earlier passes.

Same name, middle initial and city as a 2011 1128a1 ban; enrolled 2020; 2024 Part B $50,496 paid; 2024 Part D $528,832 drug cost; owner of a clinic enrolled 2026. Data match, not verified.

A NOT(a AND b...) filter silently drops rows when a middle name is NULL; it lost the $4.25M org until patched

But 143 of 999 still-designated primary-care areas were first designated 1978-89, and 31 still score 18+. That's 10 Mississippi counties (Humphreys, Jefferson, Copiah 22; Holmes 21; Sunflower, Yazoo 20), plus South Texas (Jim Hogg 23, Starr, Duval 20). Overdose join: whole counties in 18+ designations vs other counties in the same state, CDC Drug_OD 2019-24, counties with all six years counted.
results.hit_means: Named places the federal system has called severely short of doctors for 45+ years, with nothing changing. A decades-of-designation piece.
results.miss_means: Designations persist because they unlock money (NHSC, Medicare bonus), so the label outlives or overstates the gap. The overdose join had only 4 primary-care and 24 mental-health counties usable. Mental health: severe counties higher in 7 of 13 states, median ratio 1.09. traps: HPSA_FTE 0.0 with a blank formal ratio on high-needs designations may mean not counted, not zero doctors

results.headline: 420 US planes the NTSB rated destroyed still hold a valid FAA registration issued before the crash, with the same tail and serial. 344 of those crashes were fatal, with 663 dead. By crash period: 0.9% of 2008-15 wrecks, 4.1% of 2016-20, 50.4% of 2021-23, 82.5% of 2024-26. Examples (data match, not verified): N321BA, Bering Air, Nome, 2025-02-06, 10 dead, V until 2028-03-31. N93012, the B-17, Windsor Locks 2019, 7 dead, V until 2029-11-30. The triage angle itself (repeat operators and tails) is dead: fleet size explains Southwest and Air Methods, and only 63 of 1,578 Part 121/135 tails repeat.
results.checked: Took the 2,123 US N-registered aircraft the NTSB rated DEST (2008-2026) and joined them to the Aug 2026 FAA registry on N-number. Second field: the serial number must match. 632 tails are still on the registry and 470 have the same serial. 420 are status V, with the certificate issued before the crash and not expired. Where the NTSB names an owner, the first six letters match the FAA registrant 185 of 192 times. On the registry, 67% of valid rows (206,217 of 309,255) were last touched in 2023, and the top day is 2023-01-22 with 12,107. That fits the 2023 move to seven-year terms, not checked against the rule text.
results.hit_means: The registry's valid flag doesn't show whether a plane still exists. Since about 2021, planes destroyed in fatal crashes stay 'valid' for years. Owners aren't returning certificates after a total loss, and expiry was the only cleanup.
results.miss_means: It's paperwork lag with no story if the FAA deregistered file shows these cancelled while the master file lags, or if the 2021-23 planes are rebuilt wrecks.
results.boring: Paperwork lag is half ruled in: older wrecks are clean (0.9%), but half of the 3-to-5-year-old 2021-23 wrecks are still valid. Rebuilds aren't ruled out, since NTSB 'destroyed' doesn't mean scrapped, though 344 of the 420 were fatal crashes. Time since the crash muddies the before/after-2023 read, and one snapshot can't separate longer terms from less time to clean up. Next: the FAA deregistered file, the 2023 rule text, and an AIRWORTHINESS_DATE after the crash as a sign of a rebuild.
traps: OPER_NAME 'On File' is a placeholder that ranks #1 among operators with 3+ fatal events (29 events, 8 fatal)
A V on the FAA registry doesn't mean the plane exists: 420 destroyed planes are still V
162 destroyed tails are on the registry with a different serial. The N-number was reissued, so check the serial after any tail join

results.headline: Air-ambulance accidents: 59 of 184 US accidents were fatal (32.1%). The rest of Part 135: 122 of 680 (17.9%). The gap closed: 38.7% in 2008-13, 35.6% in 2014-19, 22.2% in 2020-26, while the rest of 135 held at 17-19%. LNA (Palm Beach County Park, Lantana FL) had 10 fatal in 22 accidents, 45.5% against a 13.9% baseline, z=4.29. It's the only one of 110 airports at z of 3 or more, but the 10 share no operator, aircraft or weather.
results.checked: Fatal share by type of flight for US accidents 2008-2026. The denominator is accidents in the group, counting the first aircraft per event. There are no flight hours, so these aren't true rates. Also: air medical by period, named operators with 3+ fatal events (16 of them), and airports with 15+ accidents scored against the all-airport fatal share, with a drill into the 10 LNA fatal crashes.
results.hit_means: Air ambulances crash deadlier than other charter flights, 2x in 2008-13.
results.miss_means: The gap is mostly gone (1.3x now), and no current operator stands out. The LNA crashes have nothing in common.
results.boring: Not ruled out: helicopter air-ambulance deaths were an NTSB priority and the target of the FAA's 2014 rule. Air Methods tops the list because it runs the biggest fleet. LNA is a busy coastal training field where ten unrelated private flights crashed.
traps: Deaths are 57% foreign: INJ_TOT_F sums to 16,688 but US events hold 7,166. Filter on EV_COUNTRY='USA'

menu.number: US political advertisers that gave Google only a tax ID spent $861.4M. One of them put 84% of its 2024 spend on single-gender ads.
menu.why: State races and ballot committees have no FEC ID by law, so the true dark-money slice can't be sized.

menu.lead: Nursing-home chains with repeat fire citations
menu.number: CareCore Health runs 1.95x its states' fire-citation rate, and 11 of its 12 homes repeat a tag across all 3 inspection cycles.
menu.why: Almost all sprinkler and alarm-testing paperwork, and building age isn't ruled out.

menu.lead: One man behind 630 UK companies
menu.number: An Egyptian national born in 2001 controls 630 UK companies that the register lists as live, none filing accounts.
menu.why: Probably a company-formation agent. Not-ceased control is not the same as an active company.

menu.lead: Judges with unusual bank loans hearing that bank's cases
menu.number: 68 district judges with investment-property loans, guaranties or $250K+ loans from a bank were assigned 424 cases naming that bank.
menu.why: Under the recusal law an ordinary loan isn't ownership, so most hits are routine.

menu.lead: White Birch Apartments' Section 8 rent
menu.number: HUD pays $2,574 a unit a month at White Birch in Milwaukee: 223% of fair rent, the highest of any 100+ unit building in a cheap market.
menu.why: Two tax-credit deals in seven years is the textbook setup for a legal rent reset. One strange building.

menu.lead: Medicare-enrolled orgs signed by someone with a banned person's name
menu.number: 29 enrolled orgs have a signer who shares name, state and city with a banned person. 2 of them drew $4.91M of 2024 Part B money.
menu.why: Both money names are common (Raul Rodriguez, Kevin Smith), so namesakes aren't ruled out.

menu.lead: Hospitals on ransomware leak sites
menu.number: 33 US healthcare posts on gang leak sites match a Medicare hospital by name. Watsonville Community Hospital was posted by two gangs, 10 months apart.
menu.why: A leak-site post isn't a confirmed breach, and the HHS breach portal isn't in the warehouse.

menu.lead: Altair Recycling's $57M water fine
menu.number: Altair Recycling in Texas got a $57.0M state civil penalty in June 2025, and it also has open hazardous-waste violations.
menu.why: The biggest non-BP water fine. BP's famous $6.7B is one settlement logged twice.

menu.lead: Sanctioned people controlling live UK companies
menu.number: On a strict name match, 22 sanctioned people control 46 active UK companies, and about 3 of them are likely chance.
menu.why: OFAC already named Ka On Kong's UK companies. About 7 live Kong companies OFAC didn't name is the new part.

menu.lead: Judges whose spouse drew director fees from the defendant
menu.number: 2 cases went to a judge while the judge's spouse was paid director fees by the defendant: McMahon with JetBlue, Leinenweber with P&G.
menu.why: A clean extension of F-001 but tiny: one of the cases closed in 5 days. Recusal isn't ruled out.

menu.lead: Drug-company doctor meals pile up at $125
menu.number: 47,607 doctor meals at exactly $125.00 in 2024, against 675 at $126.00.
menu.why: A fun fingerprint of company meal caps, not a harm story.

menu.lead: E-bike and moped ER visits
menu.number: E-bike and moped ER visits went from 21.8K to 87.6K, 2019 to 2023: 4x, while all injuries stayed flat.
menu.why: CPSC publishes this itself, and the 2024-25 weights changed.

menu.lead: Outside money outspent the candidates
menu.number: Outside money beat the candidate's own spending in 104 of 637 House and Senate campaigns in 2024. Moreno tops it at 5.8x.
menu.why: These are the famous Senate races, and OpenSecrets publishes the same comparison.

menu.lead: Orphaned oil and gas wells per person
menu.number: Forest County, PA has 1,685 orphaned wells per 10K people.
menu.why: Appalachian orphan wells are widely reported, and counts track how hard each state looked. There's no operator column.

menu.lead: Delaware's grip on billion-dollar bankruptcies
menu.number: Delaware holds 46 of the 80 billion-dollar Chapter 11 case families filed since 2015.
menu.why: Venue shopping is well covered, and the dollar columns failed.

menu.lead: Co-authors of retracted papers kept NIH money
menu.number: 76 co-authors of papers retracted for misconduct got $187M of NIH money after the retraction.
menu.why: Can't separate the person who faked data from the lab head. The closing skeptic read it as C.

menu.lead: Banned firms still getting federal orders
menu.number: 23 firms under a government-wide ban got $800K of orders after the ban, mostly from DoD.
menu.why: A real join, small money.

menu.lead: Hedge-fund lobbyists buying Texas meals
menu.number: Hedge funds and banks paid for 14.6% of itemized Texas lobby meals. The top name spent $10-14K over 15 years.
menu.why: Tiny money, and firms pitching state investment offices have to register.

menu.lead: NAI Logistics paid after its sanctions listing
menu.number: NAI Logistics got 13 DoD fuel actions worth a net $20,647 within 3 days of its Global Magnitsky listing.
menu.why: Probably close-out paperwork. Rank 107 is the same company from another table.

menu.lead: Oklahoma veteran suicides in 2023
menu.number: Oklahoma lost 161 veterans to suicide in 2023, against 98-134 every year from 2011 to 2022.
menu.why: One bad year, not a trend, and statistically about what the top state out of 48 shows by chance.

menu.lead: Tesla's open California OSHA cases
menu.number: Tesla has 43 accident inspections in California, 18 still open, with a median of 486 days to close.
menu.why: California codes inspections differently from other states, and there's no headcount to divide by.

menu.lead: Illinois water systems over the lead line in 2025
menu.number: 39 Illinois systems serving 887K people went over the lead limit in 2025, against at most 31 systems and 184K people in any year from 2015 to 2024.
menu.why: Round 1 already found the cause: Illinois moved 209 systems to 6-month testing in 2025. Rank 65 covers it.

menu.lead: Redlined neighborhoods and toxic plants
menu.number: 'D'-graded (redlined) 1930s neighborhoods have 13.35 toxic-release plants per 100 km2, against 2.21 in 'B' areas.
menu.why: The join works, but it's published research, and the plants likely came before the maps.

menu.lead: Black-white jail rate gap
menu.number: The median Black-to-white jail rate ratio went 4.57 (2010), 3.41 (2019), 3.86 (2023).
menu.why: This table is a copy of Vera's, and the post-2020 rise crosses a race-coding break.

menu.lead: Authors with misconduct retractions who kept NIH money
menu.number: 31 US authors with 3+ misconduct retractions got $67.1M in NIH awards after their last one.
menu.why: The same wall as F-008. It lists every author, not the one who cheated, and 4 are clearly the wrong person.

menu.lead: Big insider sales before stock collapses
menu.number: 987 of 22,770 insider months with $5M+ sold came 4-9 months before a 50%+ price drop.
menu.why: The top of the list is stock splits, and preset trading plans (10b5-1) can't be checked for these years.

menu.lead: Oklahoma refinery air penalties
menu.number: Oklahoma refineries pay $3.3K per logged violation, against $142K in Texas.
menu.why: Only 9 facilities, and states report differently to this file.

menu.lead: Eastern railroads' spill calls
menu.number: CSX and Norfolk Southern made 8.2x the spill-hotline calls of UP and BNSF in 2015-17.
menu.why: Self-reported calls with no material or amount. Reporting habit isn't ruled out.

menu.lead: EPA regions that inspect but don't act
menu.number: EPA Regions 6 and 9 have no case or informal action on file for 78% of hazardous-waste sites inspected twice or more since 2015, against 33% in Regions 7 and 8.
menu.why: The case tables carry no dates, and state enforcement isn't in them.

menu.lead: NAI Logistics paid after its ban (second table)
menu.number: NAI Logistics got 13 fuel actions worth $20.6K on or after its SAM exclusion date, paid under a different UEI.
menu.why: Same company as rank 96. The contracts are why it was sanctioned in the first place.

menu.lead: One treasurer's PACs pass little to candidates
menu.number: Datwyler's PACs send a median 16.2% of spending to candidates or outside ads, against 44.4% for peers. Only $11.1M in all.
menu.why: Leadership PACs paying for travel is legal and covered. Rank 52 is the bigger version.

menu.lead: Kings County, CA mail-ballot rejections
menu.number: Kings County, CA rejected 13.7% of returned mail ballots in 2022, against 1.52% nationally.
menu.why: The only unexplained outlier left. The codebook for its reason code isn't in the warehouse.

menu.lead: Destroyed planes re-registered after the crash
menu.number: 37 planes the NTSB rated destroyed had their FAA registration renewed or extended after the crash.
menu.why: Rebuilds or FAA batch processing fit. The 420 headline was just 7-year registration terms.

menu.lead: Banking Committee senators' bank trades
menu.number: 19% of trading senators made 34% of bank-stock trades, 2012-20.
menu.why: Perdue alone drives it. The closing skeptic read it as C.

menu.verdict: No. Nothing from the full coverage pass beats the two Medicare billing leads: F-032 (two suppliers, $593M of alginate dressings) and F-033 ($96.8M of skin substitutes for about 30 patients). Four new leads do land above ICE detainers (F-027) and the pill-death chart (F-002): the national heat-death count that lost Phoenix, SpaceX and Ford injuries for a third year, the charity-named 527s paying telemarketers, and Fast Pace's grab of new rural clinics. Environment was the richest domain by count (Nebraska air, California water surveys, chronic water-permit violators, state hazardous-waste inspectors, Iowa stack tests), health rosters gave the best named leads (Texas hospices, LA home health owners), Texas lobby filings gave the fastest ones, and energy came up empty. Still uncovered is the pitch itself, joins: pairs and hops are about 2% worked, all three tier-A findings came from those layers, and none of today's single-table leads has been joined to the money or people tables that would size it.
